articles.title: How will extreme weather in the West affect our food?
articles.summary: The impact of recent extreme heat is affecting farmers and putting pressure on our food system.
articles.body:
It has been a difficult year for farmers in the West of England as a result of the five heatwaves that have gripped the UK, scorching fields, plummeting crop yields, and leaving us in drought.

Climate scientists say extreme weather is becoming more likely , posing greater challenges to food production from farm to fork.

With a large farming industry in the region, what does this mean for the food on our plates?

"I think the consumers are going to notice that it's going to cost more money for their food," says farmer Tom Collins from Malmesbury, Wiltshire.

'Warrior' baby home after 304 days in hospital

Meningitis survivor feels 'unstoppable' on UK run

'My footballer brother hid his sexuality for years'

"There's going to be less parsnips, less carrots, less potatoes.

"All the vegetables that grow in the ground have just not had any moisture or rain on them."

It has been an "incredibly tough" summer for Collins, who has been farming for 25 years.

"I've never known a summer like it. Relentless heat every day is just exhausting," he says.

His staff have had to endure long days working in 30C heat, and the prolonged heat and dry weather have caused his spring beans to fail.

"We're probably £30,000 down on our bean income, and we've had to endure the same cost," he says.

Andrew Opie, director of food & sustainability policy at the British Retail Consortium, says extreme weather can affect crop yields and place upward pressure on prices.

"Retailers are experienced in managing supply disruptions and will take all necessary steps, including sourcing from alternative suppliers where appropriate, to minimise any impact on customers," he says.

Pete Falloon, Professor of climate resilient food systems at the University of Bristol, says the biggest challenge for food systems is likely to be the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events.

He says gradual climate changes can often be adapted to over time through changes in crop varieties or farming practices, but sudden extremes are much harder to manage.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) previously warned there could be a shortage of certain food products if drought conditions continue.

Some foods are more vulnerable than others, such as fresh fruit and vegetables, which have shorter growing cycles.

But staple crops like wheat are traded globally and benefit from storage buffers.

However, the UK imports a significant amount of food from overseas, meaning food prices and availability may be influenced by climate impacts overseas.

"Many of the places we get things like apples, oranges, berries, other vegetable crops, peppers, lettuce, in the wider Mediterranean area are also set to see significant increases in water shortages and high temperature extremes in a changing climate," says Falloon.

"The biggest impacts of things like food prices and food availability due to changing climate are likely to be on low-income groups, those living in poverty and the more vulnerable folks in society."

The UK has already experienced significant impacts from extreme weather in recent years.

This saw record-breaking temperatures, reaching up to 36.7C (98F) in Merryfield, Somerset.

According to Climate Change Committee assessments from 2025, climate-related impacts on agriculture are already costing up to billions of pounds annually.

The impacts of extreme heat extend through the food supply chain, causing stress to outdoor workers, straining refrigerating systems, changing consumer preferences and increasing food safety risks from improper storage.

Livestock suffer significantly during extreme heat, experiencing reduced productivity, health issues, and mortality.

Falloon recalls the effects of the 2022 heatwave, which led to several million premature deaths of housed poultry and increased deaths during livestock transport.

"Chicken meat production was lower partly because of animal heat stress, about 9% lower than the sort of recent average," he says.

It is projected that the UK will see hotter, drier summers and warmer, wetter winters.

But wet winters can be just as damaging as droughts.

The exceptionally wet conditions in 2024 caused difficult planting conditions for wheat , problems harvesting crops and reduced access to fields for machinery.

Falloon says these impacts can create a greater variability in food supply and potentially reduce the nutritional quality of some crops.

However, farming adaptation can help manage the impacts of extreme weather.

Debbie Wilkins, who runs Norton Court Farm, says she is learning to adapt to the changing climate.

Growing up as a child on the family-owned farm, she remembers it flooding once every five to six years.

Rather than planting arable crops on fields vulnerable to flooding, she has converted them to types of grass that are more resilient to flooding.

To mitigate the heat, she has planted more trees and hedges.

"I've always tried to be a nature-friendly mixed farm. That's helped us to be more resilient," she says.

"The type of farming I'm operating is a low-input farming, it produces less outputs but is more resilient."

Falloon says there are many practical adaptation measures already available that a growing number of farmers are engaging with.

These include planting crops earlier, using more climate-resilient varieties, improving irrigation efficiency, increasing soil organic matter, and growing deeper-rooting grasses.

"There are lots of reasons to be optimistic if we can use the information we have about future climate change, its impacts on food and farming, and work with farmers and the wider food system to understand what effective ways of building resilience might look like going forward," he says.

articles.title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
articles.summary: Using the carcinogen to preserve food is prohibited in China, the world's largest producer of cabbages.
articles.body:
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.

Officials in the north-eastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.

An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical used for preserving biological specimens that is known to cause cancer, for keeping food fresh is strictly prohibited in China.

China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.

Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.

Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.

Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.

Local authorities in Kangbao county said in a statement issued on Saturday: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."

Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.

The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.

An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."

China produces well over 30 million tonnes of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.

articles.title: Why nuclear energy is making a global comeback
articles.summary: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News.
articles.body: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News. Energy security concerns augmented by recent years of war in Ukraine and the Middle East have fueled a global resurgence of nuclear energy. In Asia, Europe, and elsewhere, governments are looking to nuclear energy as a stable power source in the face of geopolitical uncertainty, increasing electricity demand, and accelerating climate change. This includes the United States, which recently signed a thirty-year civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, though it has yet to go into effect. This resurgence marks a stunning reversal. Nuclear power development stalled after high-profile accidents such as the 1979 Three Mile Island meltdown and the 1986 Chernobyl disaster fueled public fears of the technology.

articles.title: Target reached for memorial to Channel Island WW2 journalists
articles.summary: Historian Timothy Crook says £1,000 has been raised for a memorial plaque to go in a London church.
articles.body:
A fundraising target for a memorial to Channel Islands journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two has been reached, organisers have said.

Historian Timothy Crook, who led the appeal , said the target of £1,000 was reached thanks to the "immense and wonderful generosity" of a gentleman who donated £775, plus £225 donated by members of the Chartered Institute of Journalists (CIoJ).

Journalists to be commemorated include Joseph Gillingham and Joseph Tierney who were arrested, deported and died in prison for sharing news heard on banned radios; and Frank Falla, who survived imprisonment and whose book The Silent War told how islanders challenged and outmanoeuvred censorship.

Crook, from the CIoJ, said it was hoped a plaque would be placed in St Bride's Church in Fleet Street, London, known as the "journalists' church".

Crook told BBC Jersey, if people worked in Fleet Street or around British journalism, they knew the church was something which commemorated "the courage and bravery" of those who sacrificed their lives "in the cause of their work".

"Current president Gerald Bowey is closely involved in it, and he's been very much involved in persuading the church to finally give national recognition to the enormously courageous journalists in the Channel Islands, and those ordinary people who became journalists who resisted occupation," Crook said.

He added: "When I worked in Fleet Street, I would often go to the church to say silent prayers, light candles, and remember people I've known in my career that go back 51 years in journalism that didn't come back."

Crook also thanked "brilliant historian" Prof Gilly Carr, whose "outstanding research" enabled them to recognise and appreciate the generation of journalists who achieved and "gave so much in those dark years" between 1940 and 1945.

Joe Gillingham, from Guernsey, and Joe Tierney, from Jersey, secretly spread news which often contradicted that put out through island newspapers, which were only allowed to carry war news provided and approved by German authorities.

Prof Carr said the journalists' stories were "well known" on the Channel Islands, but not so much in the UK.

She said it was great CIoJ was campaigning to have the memorial for the Channel Islanders in the church in London.

She said: "I think this memorial will be for quite a wider range of people, and I think anyone who knows grandparents might have kept a radio or who whispered the news to neighbours can feel themselves included in this because they were still spreading the news."

articles.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer Ozon targeted in Ukrainian strikes
articles.summary: Ozon says its warehouses across southern Russia, including in Dagestan and Krasnodar, were hit in the overnight strikes.
articles.body:
Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes.

Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes.

Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors".

Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals.

Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.

Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday.

The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site.

Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital.

Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.

Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan.

Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.

When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation".

The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured.

Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.

"After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn."

Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram.

Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country.

Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points.

The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.

Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population.

In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances.

But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.

This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses.

The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

articles.title: Celebrity brand whiskey distillery enters Chapter 7 liquidation
articles.summary: The distillery held a license for a massive name, and a dispute over it may have contributed to its demise.
articles.body:
While the actual decline is relatively small, even a slight drop in overall liquor sales can have a devastating impact on the industry.

"Active U.S. craft distillers dropped from 3,069 in August 2024 to 2,282 in August 2025. Seven hundred and eighty-seven fewer operations in a single year," according to The American Craft Spirits Association .

The number of active craft distillers has fallen sharply, and overall spirits sales have also declined. DISCUS CEO Chris Swonger, however, wants to put a positive spin on the decline.

"While total U.S. spirits sales edged down 2.2% in 2025, the spirits industry remains resilient, driven by innovative products that continue to spark consumer interest," he said in a press release .

"Against a challenging backdrop of weakening consumer confidence and persistent economic pressures, American adults continue to choose distilled spirits, with ready-to-drink cocktails standing out as a clear favorite."

That's one way to look at it, but the industry has been losing players, and now another distillery has filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy.

Blue Spirits Distilling filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy

While many distilleries have filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in an effort to restructure operations, Blue Spirits Distilling moved right to a Chapter 7 Bankruptcy. That means its assets will be liquidated, but exactly how that will happen remains a question.

The formal filing was made on June 11, according to court documents on Pacer Monitor , but the process remains unresolved.

"The Chelan-Douglas Regional Port Authority is waiting for the bankruptcy process to determine what happens next at the former Blue Spirits Distilling operation in the Cashmere Mill District, where the doors are locked, and company property remains inside the Port-owned facility," NCW News reported.

Another beloved beer brand files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy

Another popular brewery files Chapter 7 bankruptcy

Popular beer brand abruptly closes, liquidates everything

Although the company was based in Washington state and operated a now-closed tasting room there, its products were sold regionally. The distilleries' financial woes go back a few years.

"In 2022, commissioners approved a temporary rent deferral for Blue Spirits at the Mill District after the company reported financial challenges. At the time, Blue Spirits had made substantial investments in improvements to the Port-owned property as one of the original anchor tenants," according to NCW News.

Blue Spirits Distilling Chapter 7 at a glance

articles.title: Manga-inspired theme park to be built near Paris
articles.summary: The construction of three new parks was given the green light after a €6bn investment from Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Three theme parks will be built near Paris as part of a €6bn (£5.13bn) deal agreed between France and Saudi Arabia.

The new development is expected to include a manga-themed park, inspired by the popular Japanese franchise Dragon Ball Z.

French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the move as on a scale not seen "since Disneyland Paris", and added "you know my interest for manga".

An opening date for the parks - which will be built near Cergy-Pontoise - has not been set by the Élysée Palace, but they will open in stages and construction is expected to take years.

The project was given the green light during a two-day state visit to France by Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

It stemmed from a previous discussion between Macron and bin Salman about their shared passion for Japanese comics, "in particular Dragon Ball Z," advisers to the president told reporters on Monday.

Macron is known to be a manga fan and earlier this year ended a press briefing with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi by doing a hand gesture from the Dragon Ball series.

The project will be led by Qiddiya Investment Company (QIC) - part of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - which previously revealed plans in 2024 to build a Dragon Ball theme park near the country's capital, Riyadh.

According to local reports, the theme parks could be built on the site of the former Mirapolis park in Val-d'Oise, which closed 35 years ago.

But the deal, which the Élysée said would create about 2,000 jobs, also signals deeper ties between France and Saudi Arabia.

The leaders are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy during bin Salman's visit, which will include talks on the US and Iran conflict.

In a post on X on Sunday, Macron said bin Salman's two-day state visit marked an "important milestone".

He added that in the face of challenges in the Middle East, "France and Saudi Arabia have always worked together to promote peace and stability".

Saudi Arabia is aiming to diversify its economy away from its dependence on oil revenues, including via investment in the leisure and entertainment industry.

On Sunday, Macron hosted bin Salman at the closing of the Esports World Cup , which was due to be held in Riyadh but was moved to Paris due to safety concerns over the conflict in the Middle East.

articles.title: The grieving family who say the coroners' courts aren't working
articles.summary: One man's death highlights the growing strains on the UK's coroner's courts
articles.body:
Sarah thought she knew what she was getting into when she attended a coroner's court in May 2024 to discuss the death of her second cousin.

Her day job as a murder detective meant she was used to courts, to judges, to legal argument. What she wasn't prepared for was a coroner's court. "I felt like I was on trial," she recalls of her first hearing, in Woking, Surrey. "I remember just feeling completely railroaded… It [was] far more hostile than I had ever expected."

Her cousin, Daniel Lindsay, died in 2023, aged 41. He had lived at a home in Surrey that specialises in caring for people with learning disabilities. Daniel also had Down's syndrome and type 1 diabetes.

As his death was unexpected, his case was referred to the coroner for an inquest.

What followed was one of the most stressful experiences of Sarah's life. She discovered new details about how her cousin lived, and his cause of death. The family initially thought Daniel died from a heart attack - but over the course of the inquest, they learnt that was wrong. She had expected the process to be emotional; what she didn't predict was just how complex and frustrating it would be, at times leaving her tearful and furious.

Coroners examine deaths that are not straightforward, like unexpected or violent deaths, or those that take place in state custody. Every year, thousands of British families rely on these courts for crucial answers. For many, an inquest provides the key interaction with the arms of the state at a time of trauma.

But many observers, from MPs to legal experts, say the whole system is in peril. There are large backlogs in cases, as well as difficulties in carrying out post-mortems. As people live longer, caseloads are becoming more complex - but at the same time, resources are ever more limited, with little funding from government, regardless of party, say critics.

I've sat in various inquests over the last decade. In some, I couldn't hear the coroner through the noise of a busy train line, or because of poor acoustics in a vast room; in others, rooms became so hot that regular breaks were required.

"We're beyond crisis now," says Dr Georgia Richards, an epidemiologist at King's College London who studies the prevention of future deaths. "The government really doesn't realise the impact of the broken system."

In photos of Daniel Lindsay, two things stand out: his big smile and black hair. His family say he only had three passions in life - Chelsea, TV wrestling, and trainers. Visitors who turned up at his care home in new trainers would have to take them off so Daniel could walk around with them.

Sarah and her sister, Laura Lindsay, were Daniel's next of kin and have spent the years since his death navigating the coronial system. "Every time that we end up in court it feels as though we've got another fight," says Laura.

Coroners' courts - which operate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland - set out to answer four main questions. Three of those questions – who died, where, and when - are usually quickly answered. It's the fourth, the cause of death, that's overwhelmingly the coroner's focus.

Last year, almost 148,000 deaths were reported to coroners in England and Wales, almost a quarter of which resulted in an inquest.

After Daniel's death, the first thing the coroner did was order a post-mortem. In that regard the family was fortunate – they only had to wait a fortnight to get the results. Other coronial areas aren't so quick. Despite coroners ordering post-mortems for 51% of deaths reported to them, a dearth of pathologists willing to work for coroners is leading to huge backlogs of up to a year. There aren't enough pathologists being trained, and the basic fee of £96.80 for carrying out a post-mortem for a coroner hasn't increased in well over a decade.

Some pathologists say they get paid less than minimum wage because of the hours the work takes. "It's not just the examination. It might be reading files of hospital notes or talking to clinicians," says Dr Kathryn Griffin, an NHS pathologist in Leeds. "That's all supposed to be incorporated in the fee."

Due to the lack of pathologists, some coroners are turning to CT scanning. Popular with Jewish and Muslim families as they are non-invasive, the high-powered X-ray beams create a 3D image of the body, uncovering bone fractures or internal bleeding, for instance. "Post-mortem CT scanning [is] very good for trauma-related deaths, like a car crash," says Griffin. "It is less good for some of the reasons why people might die at home, like a clot in the lungs."

A CT scan will identify the cause of death in "about 70% of cases. [But] then you'll be left with very complex deaths and who's going to do those if you don't have well-trained autopsy pathologists?"

The government said it recognised the shortage of pathologists, but there was "no quick fix".

The merits of a post-mortem were starkly revealed in Daniel Lindsay's case. His family believed his sudden death was due to a heart attack. A phone call from the coroner's office changed all that: they were told Daniel had undiagnosed advanced oesophageal cancer, and that the main cause of death was an obstruction in his throat from some food. "So he had effectively choked," said Sarah, who didn't want to use her last name.

Of the 36,000 inquests held in England and Wales each year, only a small minority of families have legal representation; the restrictions on legal aid mean most families have to represent themselves. Institutions where people often die, such as NHS trusts or prisons, have ready access to state-funded legal teams, while many private companies choose to pay for lawyers. The new Hillsborough law should, however, make it easier for families to get legal support.

At the first court hearing, called a pre-inquest review, Sarah discovered that she was facing a legal team representing Ballater House, Daniel's care home. Feeling "railroaded" and "powerless", she left in tears and concluded the family would need their own lawyers if their questions about the care Daniel received were to be fully answered.

Daniel's family did secure legal representation after speaking to a charity. By the time his inquest opened in November 2025, they were one of several legal teams in the courtroom.

Inquests are officially meant to be inquisitorial - their aim is to find facts in a calm, sober way. But increasingly, as society becomes more litigious, they are adversarial; more like a courtroom TV drama. Despite being explicitly prevented from blaming any party for a death, hearings can often descend into a blame game, with barristers trying to save or sully an organisation's reputation. In part that's driven by lawyers realising they can use an inquest as a stepping stone to civil legal action; and by legal teams trying to ensure an organisation doesn't suffer reputational damage.

Alexia Durran, the chief coroner for England and Wales, told the BBC that coroners are seeing "increasingly complex cases" that are creating a "greater volume of work" and "greater stress" on staff.

The coroner, she says, "is not [there] to apportion blame, and so the coroner's inquest is a relatively limited one. It's not a surrogate public inquiry that is designed to answer every question."

She wants coroners to step in robustly if proceedings get too acrimonious. "The coroner should be ensuring that the family's understanding of the death is not being overtaken by advocates representing public authorities, [such as] hospitals, prisons [with] a desire to absolve themselves of responsibility, because ultimately that's not what it's about," she says.

After the revelation about Daniel's choking incident, his inquest then had to be abandoned on the second day. A former carer at the care home told the court that she had become worried about his "excessive vomiting" and had emailed her bosses about her concerns. The coroner was unaware of the email and felt further investigations would be needed.

In evidence to MPs in 2024, the former chief coroner for England and Wales, Thomas Teague KC, said the service "with very few exceptions, is chronically under-resourced and underfunded. There comes a point at which underfunding imperils the rule of law."

In a follow-up letter, MPs supported his sentiment and urged the government to invest; their pleas were turned down due to a lack of money.

One change that would not require any investment is the attitude that some coroners appear to show towards bereaved families. While I've seen some coroners check on the family daily, others have barely acknowledged them after the first day.

Daniel's family repeatedly described their coroner as being blunt and brusque, failing to put Daniel at the heart of the process. Laura said her cousin "got completely lost" in the process. The coroner who presided over the inquest, Caroline Topping, told us she was unable to comment.

Durran, the chief coroner, urges families to raise a hand or write a note if they have concerns. "Coroners are humans, they respond to human concerns."

The second inquest into Daniel's death started in June, and a month later the coroner delivered her conclusion. While finding that his care home had made some errors, she concluded that their actions had not contributed to his death. On the balance of probabilities, she ruled that Daniel had died of a choking incident caused by his undiagnosed oesophageal cancer.

Sarah and Laura were shell-shocked, and felt the conclusion had downplayed the failings in Daniel's care.

In a statement to the BBC, the care home said they respected the coroner's conclusion and extended "sincere condolences to Daniel's family", adding: "As aspects of the coronial process remain ongoing, it would not be appropriate for us to comment further at this stage."

Following the conclusion, the coroner said she was considering issuing a Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report. Such reports are written when a coroner thinks they have heard evidence that could prevent other deaths. Around 6,500 reports have been issued since the system was introduced in 2013 - but while coroners issue them, they have no power to monitor whether their recommendations are adopted.

Dr Georgia Richards, the epidemiologist, thinks those reports are too often ignored. She created and initially self-funded a "Preventable Deaths Tracker" - a system that aims to collate the reports to stop similar deaths. "The information is there, it's just not being used," says Richards. She wants coroners here to learn from her native Australia, where learning from every inquest is examined.

The Ministry of Justice says the government is considering how to strengthen the PFD system to improve oversight.

Coroners have been around so long that they're mentioned in the Magna Carta. Each day they make decisions that can help or hinder a family to understand how their relative died.

As Sarah says: "The coroner does this every day. We only do this once."

Remembering that lesson will surely help bereaved families through a process that many find bewildering at best; incomprehensible at worst.

paragraphs: Sarah thought she knew what she was getting into when she attended a coroner's court in May 2024 to discuss the death of her second cousin.

Her day job as a murder detective meant she was used to courts, to judges, to legal argument. What she wasn't prepared for was a coroner's court. "I felt like I was on trial," she recalls of her first hearing, in Woking, Surrey. "I remember just feeling completely railroaded… It [was] far more hostile than I had ever expected."

Her cousin, Daniel Lindsay, died in 2023, aged 41. He had lived at a home in Surrey that specialises in caring for people with learning disabilities. Daniel also had Down's syndrome and type 1 diabetes.
As his death was unexpected, his case was referred to the coroner for an inquest.

What followed was one of the most stressful experiences of Sarah's life. She discovered new details about how her cousin lived, and his cause of death. The family initially thought Daniel died from a heart attack - but over the course of the inquest, they learnt that was wrong. She had expected the process to be emotional; what she didn't predict was just how complex and frustrating it would be, at times leaving her tearful and furious.

Coroners examine deaths that are not straightforward, like unexpected or violent deaths, or those that take place in state custody. Every year, thousands of British families rely on these courts for crucial answers. For many, an inquest provides the key interaction with the arms of the state at a time of trauma.

But many observers, from MPs to legal experts, say the whole system is in peril. There are large backlogs in cases, as well as difficulties in carrying out post-mortems. As people live longer, caseloads are becoming more complex - but at the same time, resources are ever more limited, with little funding from government, regardless of party, say critics.

I've sat in various inquests over the last decade. In some, I couldn't hear the coroner through the noise of a busy train line, or because of poor acoustics in a vast room; in others, rooms became so hot that regular breaks were required.

"We're beyond crisis now," says Dr Georgia Richards, an epidemiologist at King's College London who studies the prevention of future deaths. "The government really doesn't realise the impact of the broken system."

In photos of Daniel Lindsay, two things stand out: his big smile and black hair. His family say he only had three passions in life - Chelsea, TV wrestling, and trainers. Visitors who turned up at his care home in new trainers would have to take them off so Daniel could walk around with them.

Sarah and her sister, Laura Lindsay, were Daniel's next of kin and have spent the years since his death navigating the coronial system. "Every time that we end up in court it feels as though we've got another fight," says Laura.

Coroners' courts - which operate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland - set out to answer four main questions. Three of those questions – who died, where, and when - are usually quickly answered. It's the fourth, the cause of death, that's overwhelmingly the coroner's focus.
Last year, almost 148,000 deaths were reported to coroners in England and Wales, almost a quarter of which resulted in an inquest.

After Daniel's death, the first thing the coroner did was order a post-mortem. In that regard the family was fortunate – they only had to wait a fortnight to get the results. Other coronial areas aren't so quick. Despite coroners ordering post-mortems for 51% of deaths reported to them, a dearth of pathologists willing to work for coroners is leading to huge backlogs of up to a year. There aren't enough pathologists being trained, and the basic fee of £96.80 for carrying out a post-mortem for a coroner hasn't increased in well over a decade.

Some pathologists say they get paid less than minimum wage because of the hours the work takes. "It's not just the examination. It might be reading files of hospital notes or talking to clinicians," says Dr Kathryn Griffin, an NHS pathologist in Leeds. "That's all supposed to be incorporated in the fee."

Due to the lack of pathologists, some coroners are turning to CT scanning. Popular with Jewish and Muslim families as they are non-invasive, the high-powered X-ray beams create a 3D image of the body, uncovering bone fractures or internal bleeding, for instance. "Post-mortem CT scanning [is] very good for trauma-related deaths, like a car crash," says Griffin. "It is less good for some of the reasons why people might die at home, like a clot in the lungs."
A CT scan will identify the cause of death in "about 70% of cases. [But] then you'll be left with very complex deaths and who's going to do those if you don't have well-trained autopsy pathologists?"
The government said it recognised the shortage of pathologists, but there was "no quick fix".

articles.title: Mortes de jogador de futebol e irmã em acidente causam comoção em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Felipe e Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 e 17 anos, estavam em carro que capotou na Rodovia Anhanguera, em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP), no domingo (23).
articles.summary: Felipe e Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 e 17 anos, estavam em carro que capotou na Rodovia Anhanguera, em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP), no domingo (23).
articles.body:
As mortes do jogador de futebol Felipe Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 anos, e da irmã dele, Beatriz Siqueira, de 17 , em um grave acidente causaram comoção entre parentes e amigos. Diversas mensagens de despedida e homenagens foram postadas nas redes sociais. (Veja abaixo).

O carro em que os irmãos estavam com a família capotou no domingo (23), na Rodovia Anhanguera (SP-330), em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP). As causas ainda são desconhecidas. A mãe deles e uma prima tiveram ferimentos graves. Veja o que se sabe.

📱 Siga o g1 São Carlos e Araraquara no Instagram

Os corpos de Felipe e Beatriz foram velados nesta terça-feira (25), no Ginásio Poliesportivo de São Bernardo do Campo . Os corpos foram enterrados durante a tarde no Cemitério Cristo Redentor em Santo André (SP).

O QUE SE SABE: entenda como foi acidente que matou jogador e irmã no interior de SP

TRAGÉDIA : Jogador de futebol de 13 anos e irmã morrem em grave acidente no interior de SP

Jogador de futebol Felipe Siqueira, de 13 anos, e a irmã, Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 17, morreram em grave acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: @maia_foto e Reprodução/Instagram

Dezenas de postagens lamentando as mortes foram postadas nas redes sociais. "Que Deus os recebam com todo amor e sejam uma linda estrela a brilhar e olhar pelos seus pais Fernanda e Nando .💔", escreveu Pati de Marco

O colégio Darwin International School, onde Felipe e Beatriz, estudavam postou nota de pesar pelas mortes.

"Há pessoas que passam por nossas vidas e deixam marcas que o tempo jamais apaga. Ficam as lembranças, os sorrisos, as histórias, os momentos compartilhados e a presença de Beatriz e Felipe na vida de tantos colegas, professores e educadores que tiveram o privilégio de caminhar ao lado deles. (...) Beatriz e Felipe, vocês serão sempre parte da nossa história e permanecerão para sempre em nossos corações. 🧡 🧡"

"Sem acreditar nessa perda tão precoce. Estamos de luto pelo Felipe Siqueira. Você é gigante menino. Você estará sempre em nossos corações e levaremos você eternamente em nossas lembranças", escreveu Miriam da Silva.

"A sua alegria jamais se apagará em nossos corações. Descansa em paz craque 😔🖤 Conforto a toda família e amigos", postou Rafael Alboccino.

Felipe Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 anos, atuava no sub-14 do Mauá Futebol Clube; ele morreu em acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro — Foto: @maia_fotoo/Instagram

Nas redes sociais, o Mauá Futebol Clube, onde Felipe atuava na categoria Sub-14, também postou nota lamentando a morte do jogador.

"Felipe fazia parte da Família Mauá Futebol e, mesmo tão jovem, já deixava sua marca dentro e fora de campo, com sua alegria e talento, compartilhando conosco momentos que permanecerão para sempre em nossa memória", afirmou.

Mauá Futebol Clube lamentou a morte do jogador Felipe Siqueira, da categoria Sub-14, em acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Facebook

Capotagem de carro em canteiro de rodovia

Família capotou no domingo (23), na Rodovia Anhanguera (SP-330), em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro — Foto: Artesp

Policiais Militares Rodoviários foram acionados para atender a ocorrência, na tarde de domingo, e constataram que o carro estava capotado no canteiro central da rodovia. O Corpo de Bombeiros chegou ao mesmo tempo e iniciou os primeiros socorros às vítimas.

De acordo com o Boletim de Ocorrência (BO), foi constatado que havia três vítimas inconscientes, uma consciente, além do condutor do veículo, um comerciante de 51 anos, pai de Felipe e Beatriz, que estava com lesões leves.

Um motorista que estava parado no acostamento e foi qualificado na ocorrência como testemunha disse à polícia que não havia nenhum outro veículo nem objeto na pista que teria causado o acidente. Ele disse que notou que o condutor perdeu o controle da direção.

Conforme o BO, o comerciante foi socorrido e levado ao Hospital Dona Balbina. Ele relatou aos policiais a mesma versão apresentada pela testemunha, de que teria perdido o controle do veículo sem nenhuma interferência externa.

Os policiais solicitaram apoio para preservação do local do acidente e foram até a Central de Polícia Judiciária (CPJ) de São Carlos (SP) noticiar o ocorrido. De acordo com o BO, o motorista não tinha sinais de embriaguez e foi submetido ao teste do etilômetro, cujo resultado foi negativo.

Durante o registro do BO, os policiais receberam a informação sobre a morte de Felipe e Beatriz, filhos do condutor do veículo.

As vítimas que tiveram ferimentos e foram socorridas são:

Maria Fernanda Siqueira Barbosa de Barros , de 46 anos (esposa do motorista e mãe das vítimas fatais): teve ferimentos graves, deu entrada no hospital consciente e passou por cirurgia em uma unidade de saúde de Ribeirão Preto (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.

Lorena Conte Barbosa Barros de Marco , de 14 anos (sobrinha do motorista): deu entrada em estado grave, inconsciente, precisou ser intubada e está internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) de um hospital de Campinas (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.

Luiz Fernando Barbosa de Barros, de 51 anos (motorista e pai das vítimas fatais): sofreu lesões leves.

articles.title: Influenciadora esfaqueia suspeito de abusar da filha em Franca, SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Ninguém foi preso. O boletim de ocorrência registra a apreensão de um canivete e aponta que a mulher também ficou ferida. A Polícia Civil apura a lesão e a denúncia de estupro de vulnerável.
articles.summary: A Polícia Civil de Franca investiga a lesão corporal e a denúncia de estupro de vulnerável após a apreensão de um canivete usado pela mulher contra o suspeito de 41 anos.
articles.body:
Uma influenciadora de 25 anos feriu com um canivete um homem de 41 anos que ela acusa de ter abusado sexualmente da filha dela, de 5 anos, na manhã de segunda-feira (24), em Franca (SP). O caso foi registrado como lesão corporal.

De acordo com o boletim de ocorrência, a ocorrência foi às 9h55 na Avenida Major Nicácio, no bairro Cidade Nova, em frente à loja onde uma tia de Laryssa Campanati Pereira trabalha. Maikel Wilker Martins, suspeito de ter cometido o abuso, foi socorrido e levado à Santa Casa.

Ninguém foi preso. O documento registra que não houve prisão em flagrante. A mulher também sofreu lesões nas costas, nos braços, nas mãos e nas pernas e foi encaminhada ao Instituto Médico Legal (IML) para exame.

A acusação de abuso sexual contra a criança foi registrada na Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM) de Franca e é apurada em investigação separada. Ele não foi preso, indiciado nem denunciado.

O g1 tentou localizar a defesa de Maikel Wilker Martins, mas não tinha conseguido até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Influenciadora golpeou com um canivete o marido da tia que é suspeito de abusar a filha de 5 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Faça parte do canal do g1 Ribeirão e Franca no WhatsApp

Segundo o documento, a mulher relatou à polícia que a filha lhe contou no dia 21 de agosto ter sido abusada sexualmente pelo homem. Ela afirmou que tentou contato com os dois conselhos tutelares da cidade e que não recebeu respaldo. Ao g1 , o conselho disse não ter recebido contato.

Ainda de acordo com o relato registrado, ela foi até a loja para contar à tia o que havia acontecido. No local, o homem teria se aproximado perguntando se ela "já sabia o que ocorrera", ido até o próprio veículo e voltado em direção a ela.

A mulher disse à polícia que, ao perceber que ele iria pegá-la à força, tirou um canivete da bolsa e desferiu um golpe. Em seguida, segundo o boletim, ele a pressionou com o próprio corpo contra o braço de um banco, e ela relatou ter desferido outros golpes em legítima defesa, enquanto pedia socorro.

O canivete foi apreendido e lacrado. A mulher informou à polícia que acredita haver câmeras de monitoramento no local. A tese de legítima defesa é a versão dela e ainda será apurada.

O homem não compareceu à delegacia porque estava em atendimento na Santa Casa. O boletim foi registrado, segundo a autoridade policial, para melhor apuração dos fatos.

Três dias entre a denúncia e o registro policial

Segundo a defesa, a criança relatou o abuso na sexta-feira (21), e o caso teria ocorrido no domingo anterior (16). A mulher levou a filha para atendimento médico no mesmo dia, e o laudo do exame foi entregue à delegacia, segundo a advogada.

A advogada afirma que a família foi informada de que a Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher de Franca funciona apenas de segunda a sexta-feira, até as 17h, e que deveria procurar o Conselho Tutelar na segunda-feira.

O registro do abuso na DDM só foi feito na segunda-feira (24), mesmo dia da agressão, de acordo com os documentos.

Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher (DDM) de Franca (SP) — Foto: Reprodução

Conselho Tutelar diz que atende 24 horas

Procurado pelo g1, o Conselho Tutelar de Franca afirmou que funciona em regime ininterrupto. "Nós atendemos 24 horas", disse uma conselheira.

Segundo o órgão, o caso só chegou ao seu conhecimento por volta das 12h de segunda-feira, pelas redes sociais, e o boletim registrado na DDM foi encaminhado ao Conselho às 14h24 do mesmo dia. Até então, não havia registro próprio sobre o caso.

O Conselho afirma que tentou contato com a mãe, sem sucesso até a entrevista, e que vai avaliar a aplicação de medidas de proteção à criança.

A lesão corporal é apurada pela Polícia Civil, e o boletim registra orientação sobre o prazo de seis meses para o oferecimento de representação criminal. A denúncia de estupro de vulnerável corre em separado, na Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher.

Denúncias de violência contra crianças e adolescentes podem ser feitas pelo Disque 100, gratuito e anônimo. Casos de violência contra a mulher podem ser denunciados pelo 180.

articles.title: Gkay escolhe chapéu de R$ 3 mil no Barretão e quer ver Simone Mendes | G1
articles.standfirst: Influenciadora participa pela primeira vez da Festa do Peão e entrou de vez no clima do rodeio. Depois de frequentar o camping e assistir a shows, ela já faz planos para voltar em 2027.
articles.summary: Gkay estreia na Festa do Peão de Barretos com chapéu de R$ 3 mil, frequenta o camping e aguarda show de Simone Mendes para encerrar sua participação no evento.
articles.body:
Estreante na Festa do Peão de Barretos, GKay parece ter entrado de vez no clima do Barretão. Nesta terça-feira (25), a influenciadora escolheu um chapéu customizado avaliado em cerca de R$ 3 mil para completar o visual e aproveitar as próximas noites no Parque do Peão, em Barretos (SP).

A peça escolhida por ela segue a estética western que toma conta do parque durante os 11 dias de festa e ganhou detalhes personalizados, inclusive joias.

Durante o passeio pela feira comercial do Parque do Peão nesta terça-feira, a influenciadora usou um look cow print que chamou a atenção dos visitantes pelo estilo.

Gkay está hospedada em um hotel no Parque do Peão desde sexta-feira (21), mas tem frequentado diariamente o camping onde estão anônimos e famosos, como Rafa Kalimann, Nattan, Ana Castela, Gusttavo Lima e Andressa Suita.

"Eu estou amando, gente. Eu já queria vir no próximo final de semana, mas não vou poder. Mas, por mim, eu ficaria aqui os dez dias. Estou amando."

Questionada se já havia se rendido também ao universo do rodeio, GKay não teve dúvidas.

"Eu sou do rodeio, eu sou da vaquejada, eu sou de onde me chamar, eu estou indo."

Gkay escolhe chapéu e customiza acessório em loja no Parque do Peão da Festa de Barretos 2026 — Foto: Thaisa Figueiredo/g1

GKay não escolheu o camping como endereço nesta primeira passagem pelo Barretão, mas a experiência por lá parece ter sido suficiente para mudar os planos para a próxima edição.

" Estou achando mara. Ano que vem eu quero vir para ficar no camping."

O camping é uma das áreas mais tradicionais da Festa do Peão e reúne grupos que praticamente se mudam para o Parque do Peão durante o evento, com barracas, motorhomes e estruturas montadas para atravessar os dias de programação.

Desde que chegou a Barretos, GKay também tem aproveitado a agenda musical.

Entre os artistas que já viu, ela destacou Ana Castela e Wesley Safadão. Gusttavo Lima, que se apresentou no sábado (22), também está entre os sertanejos citados pela influenciadora quando questionada sobre os nomes de que mais gosta.

"Ana Castela, né? Gusttavo Lima também. Amei o show do Safadão. Também amei todos os shows que eu fui. Estou apaixonada."

Gusttavo Lima comanda cavalgada com Andressa Suita e famosos pelas ruas de Barretos

Clientes pedem 'pastel do embaixador' após Gusttavo Lima encomendar 20 em barraca na feira do Barretão

Ana Castela comemora 25 milhões de seguidores com look com barriga à mostra

Os grandes shows voltam à arena na quarta-feira (26), e GKay já escolheu a atração que pretende acompanhar antes de se despedir de Barretos.

"Amanhã tem Simone Mendes, que eu estou ansiosa para ir também. Vai ser meu último show."

Ela pretende voltar em 2027 e quer trocar o hotel pelo camping para viver a festa ainda mais de perto.

articles.title: Samara Martins, candidata do partido Unidade Popular à Presidência, faz campanha em Sergipe | G1
articles.standfirst: Entre as propostas, a candidata destacou a valorização das mulheres e defendeu mudanças nas relações de trabalho.
articles.summary: Entre as propostas, a candidata destacou a valorização das mulheres e defendeu mudanças nas relações de trabalho.
articles.body:
Samara Martins , do partido Unidade Popular , fez campanha em Sergipe.

📱 Favorite o g1 no Google e acompanhe as principais notícias do dia

Acompanhada de apoiadores, a candidata participou de uma caminhada pelo Centro de Aracaju. Nas ruas da região comercial, Samara distribuiu panfletos e apresentou aos eleitores as principais bandeiras da campanha. Entre as propostas, a candidata da Unidade Popular destacou a valorização das mulheres e defendeu mudanças nas relações de trabalho:

“A nossa candidatura defende os trabalhadores, a redução da jornada de trabalho, acabar com o seis por um, o aumento de 100% do salário mínimo, acabar com os feminicídios e a violência contra as mulheres, os estupros, e isso é garantir moradia para as mulheres, garantir salário e renda para que as mulheres não dependam dos seus agressores".

Samara Martins encerrou a agenda de campanha em Aracaju participando de reunião com integrantes de movimentos sociais ligados ao direito à moradia.

articles.title: Caso Yasmin: Lucas Magalhães é condenado a 4 anos no Pará | G1
articles.standfirst: Réu, dono de lancha, vai cumprir pena com direito a recorrer em liberdade. Yasmin morreu em 2021 durante um passeio na embarcação de Lucas pelo rio Maguari.
articles.summary: Réu vai cumprir pena com direito a recorrer em liberdade. Yasmin morreu em 2021 durante um passeio de lancha pelo rio Maguari.
articles.body:
Lucas Magalhães foi absolvido nesta terça-feira (25) pelos crimes de homicídio e fraude processual no caso da morte danfluenciadora Yasmin Macêdo no Pará. Ele foi condenado pelos crimes de porte de arma e disparo de arma de fogo durante o passeio de lancha pelo rio Maguari, em Belém, em que Yasmin morreu em 2021 .

A decisão foi tomada pelo Tribunal do Júri, no Fórum Criminal de Belém . A pena aplicada foi de 4 anos e 10 meses em regime semiaberto, tendo direito de recorrer em liberdade .

Yasmin morreu em dezembro de 2021, aos 21 anos, durante um passeio de lancha pelo rio Maguari, em Belém. O corpo dela foi encontrado no dia seguinte. Segundo as investigações, a causa da morte foi afogamento.

Caso Yasmin Macêdo: Lucas Magalhães é julgado no Pará. — Foto: Reprodução / TJPA

Lucas foi submetido a júri popular para responder por homicídio com dolo eventual, fraude processual e porte e disparo ilegal de arma de fogo. A soma das penas mínimas previstas para os crimes poderia chegar a 15 anos de prisão. O acusado já estava em liberdade provisória desde 2023.

A data do julgamento foi definida após o esgotamento dos recursos apresentados pela defesa do réu em instâncias superiores, incluindo o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). Nove testemunhas foram convocadas para prestar depoimentos.

Lucas Magalhães, dono da lancha envolvida no caso Yasmin Fontes Cavaleiro de Macêdo, na época da prisão. — Foto: Felipe Bispo/Redes Sociais

Yasmin Cavaleiro de Macêdo tinha 21 anos, era estudante de medicina veterinária e também atuava como influenciadora digital. Ela desapareceu em 12 de dezembro de 2021, durante um passeio de lancha pelo rio Maguari, em Belém .

O corpo da jovem foi encontrado no dia seguinte. Segundo as investigações, a causa da morte foi afogamento.

Ao todo, 19 pessoas estavam na embarcação. Lucas Magalhães, proprietário da lancha, era apontado como principal suspeito.

De acordo com as investigações, Lucas teria efetuado disparos de arma de fogo durante o passeio e alterado a estrutura da embarcação antes da realização da perícia técnica.

O despacho da Justiça também citava outras condutas atribuídas a Lucas, descritas no inquérito policial e em procedimento administrativo instaurado pela Capitania dos Portos.

Yasmin Macêdo — Foto: Reprodução/TV Liberal

articles.title: Furto em locadora de veículos em Manaus: 4 presos por roubo de R$ 66 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Entre os presos estão duas funcionárias da empresa, que teriam facilitado o acesso dos demais suspeitos ao estabelecimento no dia do crime e fornecido informações sobre a localização do dinheiro.
articles.summary: A polícia prendeu quatro suspeitos pelo furto em locadora de veículos em Manaus, onde funcionárias ajudaram criminosos a levar R$ 66 mil do estabelecimento.
articles.body:
Suspeitos foram detidos pela Polícia Civil do Amazonas nesta terça-feira (25). — Foto: Divulgação/PC-AM

A Polícia Civil do Amazonas (PC-AM) prendeu quatro pessoas suspeitas de participação no arrombamento e furto de uma locadora de veículos no bairro Praça 14 de Janeiro, Zona Sul de Manaus . Entre os presos estão duas funcionárias da própria empresa que, segundo as investigações, teriam facilitado a entrada dos criminosos no estabelecimento.

O crime ocorreu na madrugada de sexta-feira (21). De acordo com a PC-AM, Ana Vitória Vasconcelos Nascimento e Maira Maria Silva de Moraes, funcionárias da empresa furtada, teriam deixado portas de acesso à área de escritórios deliberadamente abertas para facilitar a ação dos demais suspeitos.

Ainda conforme a investigação, horas antes do crime, Ana Vitória teria feito uma chamada de vídeo com um dos envolvidos e indicado o local onde estava guardada uma quantia de R$ 66 mil. Durante a investigação, os policiais também encontraram um notebook pertencente à empresa que também havia sido furtado.

📲 Participe do canal do g1 AM no WhatsApp

Renato Carvalho, Ana Vitória e Maira Maria foram presos preventivamente. Já Pedrinho da Silva Pereira foi preso em flagrante. A PC-AM também cumpriu três mandados de busca e apreensão, incluindo um relacionado à motocicleta que teria sido utilizada no crime.

Os quatro devem responder por associação criminosa e furto qualificado. Pedrinho também foi autuado por tráfico de drogas, associação para o tráfico e receptação.

Após os procedimentos policiais, os suspeitos passarão por audiência de custódia e ficarão à disposição da Justiça.

Ainda conforme a investigação, horas antes do crime, Ana Vitória teria feito uma chamada de vídeo com um dos envolvidos e indicado o local onde estava guardada uma quantia de R$ 66 mil. Durante a investigação, os policiais também encontraram um notebook pertencente à empresa que também havia sido furtado.

Renato Carvalho, Ana Vitória e Maira Maria foram presos preventivamente. Já Pedrinho da Silva Pereira foi preso em flagrante. A PC-AM também cumpriu três mandados de busca e apreensão, incluindo um relacionado à motocicleta que teria sido utilizada no crime.
Os quatro devem responder por associação criminosa e furto qualificado. Pedrinho também foi autuado por tráfico de drogas, associação para o tráfico e receptação.
Após os procedimentos policiais, os suspeitos passarão por audiência de custódia e ficarão à disposição da Justiça.

articles.title: TRE suspende determinação para cassação de mandato de vereador da BA  | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão que suspende a determinação para a cassação do mandado de Diogo Azevedo foi divulgada pelo órgão nesta terça-feira (25).
articles.summary: Decisão que suspende a determinação para a cassação do mandado de Diogo Azevedo foi divulgada pelo órgão nesta terça-feira (25).
articles.body:
O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Bahia (TRE-BA) determinou, em uma decisão divulgada nesta terça-feira (25), que o vereador de Vitória da Conquista , Diogo Azevedo, permaneça no cargo. O órgão havia determinado, em primeira instância, a cassação do mandato do político em um processo por infidelidade partidária.

Conforme informações apuradas pela TV Sudoeste, afiliada da TV Bahia na região, a nova decisão foi tomada pela desembargadora Carina Cristiane Canguçu Virgens. A magistrada suspendeu os efeitos da cassação até que os embargos de declaração sejam devidamente julgados pelo colegiado do TRE-BA.

Em novo entendimento, a desembargadora afirmou que decisões que determinam a perda de mandato eletivo só devem ser executadas quando não restarem recursos nas instâncias superiores. À TV Sudoeste, Diogo Azevedo afirmou que recebe a decisão com tranquilidade e que confia na Justiça.

📲 Clique aqui e entre no grupo do WhatsApp do g1 Bahia

TRE-BA cassa mandato do vereador Diogo Azevedo — Foto: Câmara Municipal de Vitória da Conquista

Na decisão do dia 13 de agosto, a Justiça Eleitoral entendeu pela cassação do mandato do vereador e considerou que ele cometeu infidelidade partidária após deixar o União Brasil e se filiar ao Partido da Social Democracia Brasileira (PSDB) sem apresentar uma justificativa legal válida para a troca de legenda.

Na ocasião, o tribunal rejeitou as alegações apresentadas pela defesa de que Diogo teria sido vítima de perseguição e de conflitos políticos internos no antigo partido. O político teve um prazo de cinco dias, a partir da divulgação da decisão, para apresentar o recurso e pedir a suspensão dos efeitos da determinação do TRE-BA.

Apesar da decisão, o vereador não perde o mandato imediatamente. O afastamento depende da publicação do acórdão, documento que formaliza o julgamento. Diogo Azevedo foi eleito em 2024 como o vereador mais votado da história de Vitória da Conquista.

O caso já havia provocado uma mudança temporária na composição da Câmara Municipal. Em julho, uma liminar determinou o afastamento de Diogo Azevedo e a convocação do suplente Alisson da Educação.

A medida, no entanto, foi suspensa pouco depois, e o vereador permaneceu no cargo até o julgamento do mérito pelo TRE-BA.

Com a decisão do último dia 13 de agosto, o tribunal voltou a determinar a perda do mandato, mas os efeitos práticos ainda dependiam das etapas formais do processo e dos recursos que serão apresentados pela defesa.

articles.title: Cabo Frio: adolescentes com 12 e 8 passagens pela polícia tentam fuga | G1
articles.standfirst: Dupla foi apreendida nesta terça-feira (25) no bairro Porto do Carro com cocaína, maconha e crack, segundo a PM.
articles.summary: Dupla foi apreendida nesta terça-feira (25) no bairro Porto do Carro com cocaína, maconha e crack, segundo a PM.
articles.body:
Adolescentes foram apreendidos após tentarem se esconder em uma padaria em Cabo Frio — Foto: Região dos Lagos Notícias

Dois adolescentes foram apreendidos por ato análogo ao tráfico de drogas nesta terça-feira (25), após tentarem fugir da Polícia Militar e se esconderem dentro de uma padaria no bairro Porto do Carro, em Cabo Frio , na Região dos Lagos do Rio. Com eles, foram apreendidos cocaína, maconha e crack.

Segundo a Polícia Militar, os adolescentes foram vistos durante um patrulhamento na comunidade carregando sacolas. Ao perceberem a presença dos agentes, os dois correram e, durante a fuga, entraram em uma padaria na tentativa de se esconder.

Os policiais seguiram os adolescentes até o estabelecimento e conseguiram alcançá-los.

De acordo com a ocorrência, durante a fuga, um deles arremessou a sacola que carregava para dentro de uma caixa. No recipiente, os agentes encontraram drogas e dinheiro. O segundo adolescente foi abordado ainda com a sacola que carregava.

📱 Siga o canal do g1 Região dos Lagos no WhatsApp.

Ao todo, foram apreendidos 67 pinos de cocaína, com 147 gramas; 58 buchas de maconha, totalizando 168 gramas; e duas pedras de crack, com um grama. Um aparelho celular e R$ 17 em dinheiro também foram recolhidos.

A Polícia Militar informou que os dois adolescentes já possuem registros anteriores por atos análogos a crimes relacionados ao tráfico. Segundo a corporação, um deles acumula 12 registros por tráfico, enquanto o outro possui oito registros por tráfico e associação para o tráfico.

Os adolescentes e o material apreendido foram encaminhados à 126ª Delegacia de Polícia. Após a apresentação da ocorrência à autoridade policial, os dois permaneceram apreendidos.

articles.title: Somerset cider makers left with very few apples after heatwaves
articles.summary: Some orchards are harvesting just a 10th of their usual crop, and facing an uncertain future.
articles.body:
Somerset's famous cider orchards have been "decimated" by the long summer drought, producers say. Many trees have produced no fruit at all, and others have dropped their fruit early, rotting before they ripened.

"It's gut-wrenching," says Kimberly Jones of Honey's Cider near Bath, whose orchard has produced only a 10th of its normal amount of apples.

Neil MacDonald, who manages more than 1,000 acres of Somerset orchards, says he has watched half his apples fall before they have ripened, because the trees are stressed by the drought.

"Nothing sells cider like sunshine," he says, "and we've emptied our tanks.

"The sadness is we haven't got enough fruit to refill the tanks again."

Teenagers arrested after fire destroys businesses

Funds needed to repair war memorial pavilion

Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts

Walking through Kimberly Jones' orchard just outside Bath, it's hard to see any apples at all. The trees should be groaning with fruit, she tells me, but "we might get 10% of our normal crop here, and that's generous".

The orchard is 25 years old, and this is by far the driest year they have had. Because 2025 was also dry, the trees became stressed, she explained, and this year most have just not made fruit at all, to save their energy.

Unlike the big commercial brands, Honey's Cider is only made from fresh juice. Jones refuses to buy apple concentrate or industrial products.

"So we can only make cider from the juice we make each year, which means we will be down this year," she adds.

Ironically, the long hot summer has been "brilliant" for actually selling cider.

"Everyone likes a cold cider on a hot day, but we are struggling now to grow fruit for next year," Jones says.

On one of Somerset's most famous cider farms, I hear the same story. Gordon Rich started pressing apples on a farm near Highbridge in 1954. Today his grandson George Scott makes nearly a million litres of cider a year.

"We would normally harvest 20-30 tonnes of apples here," he tells me, walking through one orchard.

"There's so little fruit in here I won't even put the harvester in - the sheep can have any that drop."

Neighbouring farms that Scott buys from are also short of fruit. One grower who normally produces 200 tonnes is "down to about 30", he adds.

Will his tanks run dry then, I wondered?

"No, we've got plenty of cider in the tanks for now," he smiles. Cider makers can keep stock from year to year, but Scott says he worries about the future of his trees.

Two years of drought have already stressed them, and climate scientists are warning farmers to expect more hot dry summers .

"I do worry that next year will show a lot more signs of the drought and the trees will be stressed again. If we get another dry year, I don't know what we're going to do," he adds.

Not every orchard is bare, of course. Neil MacDonald manages more than 1,000 acres of cider orchards across Somerset. At his Orchard Park Farm, near Shepton Mallet, I see plenty of apples - both on the trees and on the ground.

With a roar, the apple harvester starts up. It powers down the rows, sweeping up the apples under the trees, up and away into the trailer.

This is at least three weeks' early for harvest, but they are not picking up the fruit to make cider.

"All these apples will go on the compost heap," MacDonald tells me, ruefully.

He cuts one open to show me the inside, mottled brown and floury.

"It's unripe, but it's already rotted before we've even started," he explains.

"The trees are stressed without any water, so they've just dumped the fruit on the ground to save themselves."

The harvester sweeps along, filling a large trailer with cider apples that Neil and his team have spent all year trying to grow, only to throw away.

"We've probably lost about half the crop this way," he says.

"This should be a 20-tonne orchard. If I get 10 tonnes from it I'll be grateful."

Somerset's cider apple growers know this is not a freak year.

"What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal." says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office .

But what can an apple grower do about it?

Neil MacDonald is now watering newly planted trees.

"Five years ago you would just dig a good hole and leave nature to get on with it," he smiles.

"Now you can't get away with that, you have to irrigate young trees or they die."

But irrigation for hundreds of acres of cider orchards is "just not viable", he said. Farmers who grow eating apples for supermarkets command higher prices for their fruit, so traditionally they have invested in irrigation systems.

Cider growers are now having to rethink their calculations.

Most fundamentally of all, climate change may actually change the taste of West Country cider.

One of the main varieties that gives Somerset cider its bittersweet taste is Dabinett. Several growers have found these trees producing very few apples this year, not because of the drought, but the mild winter.

"Dabinett needs a cold snap," MacDonald explains. "We just didn't get the cold winter days this year or last, so it's not producing."

He is now grafting other varieties onto his Dabinett trees, plants that fare better in hot dry weather.

As our climate changes, the very taste of Somerset cider may change too.

articles.title: British man charged in Singapore two years after alleged theft at Changi airport
articles.summary: The 26-year-old faces up to seven years in jail for allegedly stealing a denim jacket from an airport shop in 2024.
articles.body:
Singapore has charged a British man for theft more than two years after he allegedly stole a denim jacket from a store at the airport shopping mall.

The police were alerted to the theft in the evening of 14 August 2024 when a retail assistant at Singapore's Changi Airport realised a blue denim jacket was missing from a display mannequin.

Surveillance footage showed a man removing the jacket, worth about S$350 ($275; £202), from the mannequin and leaving the store without making payment. By the time the authorities established his identity, the man had departed Singapore.

The 26-year-old was arrested on 15 August this year while in transit at the airport and was charged on Tuesday.

"The police take a serious stance of shop theft and will deal firmly with offenders in accordance with the law.

"Offenders should not assume that they can evade detection simply by leaving Singapore after committing an offence," the Singapore Police Force said in a statement on Monday.

In its statement the police also recounted a separate arrest of a 50-year-old Polish woman who had stolen two bottles of perfume from retail stores inside one of the airport's terminals on 11 June this year.

She was arrested in the transit area shortly before she was scheduled to depart Singapore. The woman was charged with two counts of theft on Tuesday.

Those convicted of theft in Singapore face up to seven years in jail.

articles.title: Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling âsoft minority appeasementâ? Or has the party played to BJPâs strength by la.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling âsoft minority appeasementâ? Or has the party played to BJPâs strength by lapping up a controversy that may push it into a corner?The Congress's decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party events signalled a rare hardening of stance on an issue that the party knows could make it vulnerable to attacks over both minority appeasement and nationalism.As expected, the Congress decision, which cited a 1937 resolution, triggered sharp reactions from the BJP, with Union home minister Amit Shah accusing the Congress of repeating "politics of appeasement."Union minister JP Nadda also slammed the Congress, alleging that the party's 1937 resolution was driven by "appeasement politics" and contributed to the circumstances that led to the Partition. In a post on X, Nadda said the Congress' decision in 1937 to divide 'Vande Mataram' into two parts fuelled the two-nation theory and ultimately led to the partition of the country.'This was followed by attacks questioning Congressâs commitment to nationalism and patriotism.Union minister Giriraj Singh accused the Congress leadership of disrespecting the legacy of India's freedom fighters and operating under ideological pressure. "This is not just opposition to Vande Mataram but against our revolutionaries," Singh said, adding, "Now, the Congress has become the Muslim League. This is not Gandhi ji's Congress but Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi's Congress," the BJP leader said.BJP MP Dinesh Sharma also accused the opposition leadership of harbouring "Muslim League-like thinking." He equated senior Congress leaders with Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan who spearheaded the Two-Nation Theory, to criticise the Congress party's approach toward national symbols.Later, the BJP passed a resolution condemning the Congress Working Committee's decision to sing only the first two stanzas of 'Vande Mataram' and announced a nationwide campaign to raise awareness about the history and significance of the National Song.No surprises here. All these attacks were on expected lines. Surely, the Congress would have anticipated these high-pitched narratives questioning its nationalism and accusing it of appeasement.Congress fights backCongress leaders defended the party's stand, saying 'Vande Mataram' was associated with the freedom struggle and held emotional significance for the Congress. They accused the BJP of politicising the issue and diverting attention from the issue of Ram Mandir donation theft."BJP was not a part of the freedom struggle. Vande Mataram was a part of the freedom struggle; it is emotional for us, but political for them (BJP)," Venugopal said, adding, "We have been reciting Vande Mataram since 1937, more than 90 years. What is new for us?"The Congress leaders alleged that political rivals led by the BJP were deliberately stoking nationalist narratives to cover up their failures. What the Congress perhaps did not realise, or chose to ignore, was that the BJP had already set the stage for bringing Vande Mataram to the centrestage of its politics.Why the 1937 reference created more problems than it solvedBankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote âBande Mataramâ in the late 19th century in Sanskritised Bengali. The original version consisted of six stanzas. The song was first inserted into the pages of his novel, Anandamath, set during the late 18th century when famine and rebellion tore through Bengal.In 1950, alongside âJana Gana Manaâ as the national anthem, Vande Mataram received the honour of a national song following a decision of the Constituent Assembly, under the guidance of Rajendra Prasad, considering the historic role it played in Indiaâs freedom struggle.However, only the first two stanzas of the song were adopted as the national song.The Congress Working Committee (CWC), in a resolution of October 29, 1937, decided that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at national and public gatherings.This had followed advice from Rabindranath Tagore, who was the first to set Vande Mataram to music and publicly sing it at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. However, as the Congress lost political heft, the minorities gradually shifted to other regional parties. The same happened with other social groups like the SCs, STs and the OBCs. For the last many years, the Congress has been forced to align with the regional parties that weaned away its core voters. Now, as it tries to script its revival, it is trying to win back these communities into the party fold.We have seen Rahul Gandhi aggressively woo the SCs, STs and the OBCs by repeatedly taking up issues that impact them. The Congress leaderâs sustained pitch for caste census was an open move to reach out to these core voters. And itâs not just the Muslim appeasement attack that the Congress wants to avoid, it perhaps also does not want to antagonize its ally in Uttar Pradesh - the Samajwadi Party. Interestingly, Rahul and Akhilesh Yadav appeal to the same social support base and hence the alliance chemistry is always overshadowed by competing interests.It is in this context that one is left wondering: Has the Congress taken a calculated gamble?Get the latest India News and Live updates.
