articles.title: Man jailed for killing Leicester student over fake Rolex row
articles.summary: Harper Dennis was found guilty of manslaughter following a two-week trial at Leicester Crown Court.
articles.body:
A student who stabbed his former friend through the heart in Leicester after they fell out over a fake Rolex watch has been found guilty of manslaughter and jailed.

Harper Dennis, 19, plunged a knife five times into the chest of Khaleed Oladipo, 20, near De Montfort University in Leicester on the evening of February 3 this year.

A jury at Leicester Crown Court found Dennis not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter, having an offensive weapon and failing to provide the pin to his phone after a two-week trial on Tuesday.

Dennis, of Bath Lane, Leicester, was sentenced to a total of 10 years' imprisonment.

Prosecutor Jane Osborne KC told the jury Dennis killed Oladipo, who he made friends with through online gaming, because of a "perceived debt".

The trial heard their friendship soured after an unsuccessful attempt by Dennis to sell a fake Rolex given to him by Oladipo.

Judge Timothy Spencer KC told Dennis, who wore a dark suit in the dock, he had developed a "seething resentment" towards the victim.

He said: "You took a knife to the fight, you used it, this was not a one-off thrust of the knife but five separate applications and it should have been obvious to you this carried a high risk of serious harm."

He added: "The background is murky. You and Khaleed were certainly known to each other. You were probably, at times, pretty friendly.

"The moral high ground is simply not open to you. You have painted yourself as wronged, but the reality is the financial transactions in this case were all to do with scams.

"This money was designed to fund criminal activity. The dispute between the two of you was further fuelled by him providing a Rolex watch which you viewed as some part compensation for your losses, that turned out to be fake and that did not assuage your bitterness."

The judge said both Dennis and Oladipo had their "lives ahead of you".

He said: "This is not a case of a single desperate stab wound – this is one of five thrusts of the knife. You knew you had something serious in mind because you covered your face immediately before."

Oladipo's sister Precious Oladipo said in a victim impact statement that their mother had become withdrawn because she was "so unwell with grief".

She said: "The loss of a child is brain-altering. He was, in every sense, her light and joy and losing him has hollowed her out.

"She cries every single day, including at her workplace, the hospital. She mumbles that she sent Khaleed off to university, as she always did after the holidays, and he simply never came home."

She added: "The home we shared that was once full of laughter is now largely silent.

"Khaleed will not graduate, he will not see his 21st birthday, which he had been so looking forward to. Every future milestone will now be marked by his absence instead of his presence.

"We are bereft, there is no joy or happiness in our home. We move through life monotonously.

At about 17:00 GMT on the night he died, Oladipo left his girlfriend's flat carrying a plastic bag of leftover snacks and was on the phone to her while he walked back to his accommodation nearby to watch football.

But outside the De Montfort University's Innovation Centre, he was met by Dennis who was captured on CCTV walking up and down in the "busy" area.

"It took less than 30 seconds for the two men to come together, to struggle and for the defendant to leave," Osborne told the court.

The court was told Oladipo's girlfriend heard him say "why did you come up and stab me?" over the phone before asking for her to call the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination showed he had suffered six wounds, five to the chest including one which penetrated his heart, and one to his thumb.

Despite being taken to the Leicester Royal Infirmary, he was pronounced dead just over an hour after the stabbing, which took place near the DMU campus.

Giving evidence in his defence on Wednesday , Dennis said he was "fearful" for his life when Oladipo approached him with a knife, adding he was "wrestling" to prevent the 20-year-old from stabbing him.

In cross-examination, prosecutor Jane Osborne KC asked if Dennis knew he had stabbed Oladipo, to which he replied: "I didn't know and I didn't know he was hurt, and I didn't intend to cause any serious harm."

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Oladipo and Dennis walking towards each other, with Osborne suggesting Dennis used his hands to open a folding knife.

Dennis denied the suggestion he had a knife in his possession, and said he did not leave his accommodation with one.

Addressing Dennis, the prosecutor said there was "bad feeling" between Dennis and Oladipo - and suggested Dennis left his accommodation with a knife "to settle it".

Dennis, who was a first-year business management student at the University of Leicester, told jurors he had been talking to Oladipo - who was in his third year at DMU - about money and "doing fraud".

He said: "Khaleed initiated it - saying that there are ways you can make money, and with these methods you will gain large amounts of profit through it, through these websites."

Dennis said he wanted to "make some profit", so sent Oladipo £6,000 - from his savings and money his parents had given him - but did not get his money back.

The defendant said Oladipo gave him a Rolex watch. Dennis added: "He said that the watch is real and you will be able to sell it and make the money back from it."

Dennis, the court heard, took the watch to a jewellers in Hatton Garden in Camden, London, and "was laughed at".

"Two jewellers looked at the watch, they examined it and realised it was fake," Dennis said.

"It made me feel a bit annoyed, bit kind of disappointed in Khaleed that he let me down."

Dennis, who told the court he had a gambling addiction, said he threatened to expose Oladipo online as someone who "can't be trusted" and a "bad businessman".

Det Insp Lorna Granville, from the East Midlands Special Operations Unit Major Crime Team, said: "It's a shocking set of circumstances and quite rightly, and expectedly, creates a huge impact on the student community.

"This is not deep entrenched criminality.

"What it appears is two young men with their lives ahead of them have had a falling out and one has reacted, I would say, completely disproportionately and unnecessarily to exact some retribution".

articles.title: Former South Wales Police officer charged with raping and strangling woman in Swansea
articles.summary: Rikki Hall, 33, was on duty in Swansea when he allegedly attacked the woman, the police watchdog said.
articles.body:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

articles.title: Germany's Merz warns attackers will 'pay price' after drone incident
articles.summary: A drone attack on Leipzig Airport highlights the "very real threat" faced by the country, the German chancellor says.
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that those responsible for drone attacks and other hostile acts against Germany, including a recent case at Leipzig Airport, would "pay a price".

Merz said the incident showed Germany was "facing a very real threat" and was increasingly becoming a target.

On 4 August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty.

Police defused the explosives and believe a second drone may have collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. Security experts have speculated that Russia may have been responsible.

The German government has made no direct accusations. Moscow has denied involvement.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carry most of the country's aerial cargo. It is also a major hub for logistics group DHL.

"We have problems, some of which stem from outside the country, and which we must not ignore," Merz said.

"Attackers are increasingly ruthless, accepting even severe property damage, and even injuries and fatalities."

According to German reports, investigators have since found a third drone near Leipzig airport.

Public broadcasters NDR, WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper also reported that traces of the military explosive hexogen were found nearby.

Speaking on the margins of a government coalition retreat at Neuhardenberg, Merz said the government was working closely with the security authorities on the case and would release more details soon.

Merz also vowed to "stay the course" supporting Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion.

"The government is continuing its support for Ukraine with steadfast resolve," he said. "Today, we are its strongest supporter - not to prolong the war, but to force peace talks."

Germany, he said, was initiating a range of measures to better protect itself against such attacks.

These include stronger drone defences and plans to empower security services to strike back against attackers at home and abroad, for example by hacking their computer servers.

There has been a series of unauthorised drone flights in recent months over sensitive sites in Germany including military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies.

Police have warned that the overflights could have been organised by Russian agents.

"The government is continuing its support for Ukraine with steadfast resolve," he said. "Today, we are its strongest supporter - not to prolong the war, but to force peace talks."
Germany, he said, was initiating a range of measures to better protect itself against such attacks.
These include stronger drone defences and plans to empower security services to strike back against attackers at home and abroad, for example by hacking their computer servers.
There has been a series of unauthorised drone flights in recent months over sensitive sites in Germany including military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies.
Police have warned that the overflights could have been organised by Russian agents.

articles.title: Man spots wallaby hopping around English countryside
articles.summary: "You're not from around here, are you?" The post Man spots wallaby hopping around English countryside appeared first on Talker.
articles.body:
A wallaby has been spotted hopping around the Cornwall, England countryside.

Scot Weller was driving into Liskeard when he saw what he initially thought was a dog in the road ahead.

The owner of Original Cornish Pasties says the animal was jumping along the road in front of him as he drove to work.

No one knows how the marsupial native to Australia ended up in Cornwall.

Last month, a wallaby was also spotted in north Devon .

Scott said there were several cars behind him and, worried the animal could be hit, he decided to follow it.

The wallaby then made its way onto the sidewalk and stopped.

He said: "But then I realized it was hopping and that it was a wallaby on the loose."

Scott pulled alongside and said to the escaped marsupial: "Hello, you're not from around here, are you?"

The animal then disappeared down a side road toward the local Co-op.

"It was a bit sad that he was out there on his own, as there can't have been much for it to eat because of the heatwave we've been having ," Scott said.

"I just thought, 'Poor thing, he's lost.'"

He reported the sighting to police via 101, although the call handler initially had some trouble comprehending what he was reporting.

"I told her, 'There's a wallaby hopping up the street,' and she replied, 'The Australian animal, like a small kangaroo? Right, OK.'"

The wallaby has reportedly been sighted elsewhere in Liskeard.

A member of staff at the leisure center is also said to have spotted it at the weekend in the secondary school playing fields.

A Devon and Cornwall Police spokesperson said that the animal had disappeared by the time officers arrived.

They said: "We were called to a report of a wallaby seen on Dean Street, Liskeard, shortly before 6am today, August 24. Officers carried out an area search but did not locate the animal."

articles.title: India, China to work towards political settlement of boundary question in long-term interests; Beijing stresses package solution
articles.summary: India News: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month, India and China held the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) Dialogue on the.
articles.body: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month, India and China held the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) Dialogue on the Boundary Question, endorsing efforts to formalise the recent turnaround in the relationship on the back of border peace and discussing issues like de-escalation, boundary demarcation and border management.After the talks chaired by Special Representatives Ajit Doval and Wang Yi, while India said both sides agreed to work towards a political settlement of the boundary question in their long-term interests, Beijing also recalled a 2005 bilateral agreement to stress its proposal for a package solution.Doval was quoted as saying by the Chinese side that India and China are partners, not competitors, and developing a stable, predictable, and forward-looking India-China relationship carries great significance also for Asia and the world.âThe normalcy we have witnessed in our relationship has been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas,â said Doval, stressing the significance of border peace for further progress in bilateral ties. Wang, however, reiterated Chinaâs position that the border issue must be placed in an âappropriate positionâ in ties.According to a Chinese readout, Doval and Wang held "in-depth communications" on advancing boundary demarcation negotiations, improving border management and control and promoting cross-border cooperation, while reaffirming their commitment to the 2005 agreement on political parameters and guiding principles for a "fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable package settlement" to the boundary question.China had dropped the mention of package settlement, which seeks a quid-pro-quo approach, in its readout of the last round of talks but had used it regularly for SR meetings earlier. Indian governments in the past, like in 2007 in Parliament, have said that they were exploring a "final package settlement" covering all sectors of the boundary under the 2005 bilateral agreement but India has not used that formulation recently, stressing instead on a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement framework.On this occasion, the Indian government said in a statement that under the strategic guidance of PM Narendra Modi and President Xi, - in a constructive and forward-looking spirit â Doval and Wang had a candid exchange of views and agreed to continue their work in seeking a "political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests".The SR talks took place ahead of likely back-to-back bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi - first in Kyrgyzstan on the margins of the upcoming SCO summit and second at the BRICS summit that India will host on September 12-13. Xi is expected to arrive in India on September 12 for his first visit to the country in 7 years. While the schedule is yet to be confirmed, official sources said he will have a bilateral meeting with Modi and attend the PM's welcome dinner for BRICS leaders on September 12, before participating in the BRICS summit the next day.On the boundary issue, the Chinese side further said that both countries agreed to properly handle the boundary question through dialogue and consultation, jointly safeguarding peace and tranquility in the border areas.According to Beijing, Wang said that China-India relations have surpassed the bilateral scope and hold global and strategic significance and pointed to consensus reached in Modi-Xi metings in Kazan and Tianjin."China is willing to join hands with India to grasp bilateral relations from a strategic height and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, enhance understanding, resolve differences, overcome obstacles, and serve as good neighbors, friends, and mutually enabling partners, thereby realizing the vision of the Dragon-Elephant Tango," said Wang.Doval also called on Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng during the visit and discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquility in the border areas and further improve bilateral relations across economic, political and multilateral forums.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Canada unveils counter-tariffs of 15-50% on US goods
articles.summary: Canada on Tuesday announced counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent, intensifying the trade war between the historically close allies.T...
articles.body:
Canada on Tuesday announced counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent, intensifying the trade war between the historically close allies.

Ottawa's retaliation will take effect September 8, a timeframe earlier outlined by Prime Minister Mark Carney after US President Donald Trump's 50-percent duties came into place Saturday.

The retaliatory tariffs of 15 percent, 25 percent or 50 percent match US levels, said Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne. They impact industries including steel, dairy and electronics.

The list includes frozen and fresh fish, consumer goods like dishwashers and washing machines, as well as industrial products including railway construction materials.

Canada's government also announced a $5.4 billion (CA$7.5 billion) aid package for firms and workers.

"This is an unprecedented challenge imposed on Canada. But Canada will meet the moment," Champagne added. "I think what Canadians can see this morning is that we stand united."

Industry Minister Melanie Joly echoed Champagne's call for Canadians to support local businesses, vowing to work with new allies and trading partners.

She also pledged to "fight back" if Trump raised US tariffs on Canadian autos to 50 percent.

Trump's latest tariffs hit about $20 billion in Canadian goods -- or 5.5 percent of its exports to the United States -- after trade negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour.

Under Canada's planned response, US steel and aluminum products previously subject to a 25-percent duty will soon face 50-percent tariffs.

Goods facing 25-percent tariffs include appliances, dairy products like cheese, as well as certain steel and aluminum derivative products.

A small category will see a 15-percent duty, including electric equipment and tools.

These form about 7.3 percent of Canada's imports from the United States at 2024 levels.

But analysts warn of tit-for-tat escalation.

Already on Monday, Trump pledged to double tariffs on Canadian autos starting 2027, up to 50 percent from the current 25 percent for non-US content.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticized Trump's threat, saying he could "kiss my ass" and threatening an electricity export surcharge.

Trump lashed out at Ford and also referred to Carney as a "governor," re-upping his inflammatory push for Canada to become the 51st US state.

Highlighting the animosity, Trump said Tuesday he was considering renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

The fresh US tariffs do not exempt products under the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement. They raise the US effective tariff rate on Canadian exports to 6.9 percent from 5.1 percent, Oxford Economics estimates.

Tariffs on plastics, electrical machinery, and wood and paper products contribute most to the increase.

"Manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be affected the most," Oxford Economics said.

The exchanges drew some concern in the United States. Ethan Johnson, 25, who runs a start-up, told AFP: "The economics and the math behind it do not make sense."

But 29-year-old electrician Lucas Feser trusts the Trump administration "to set up a harder, better deal."

Carney previously said US negotiators sought restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the last minute.

US officials made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture" too, he added, referring to eastern Canada's French-speaking province.

Trump pushed back Tuesday, saying on Truth Social that he would "never interfere with Canadians speaking French." He accused Carney of lying for political support.

The United States is Canada's biggest trading partner. Canadian exports to its neighbor represent 70 percent of its overall total.

Canada is the second-biggest US trading partner in goods this year behind Mexico.

Polling released Sunday by the Angus Reid Institute showed Canadians broadly support Carney's move to walk away from talks, but some fear economic repercussions.

The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in rolling out new tariffs.

articles.title: Female Virginia officer sues police department after allegedly sharing locker room with biological male
articles.summary: Former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow sued her police department earlier this month after sharing a women's changing room with a biological male in 202...
articles.body:
A former Norfolk, Virginia , police officer filed a lawsuit against the city and its police chief earlier this month after the police department allegedly allowed a biological male to use the women's locker rooms.

According to the documents obtained by Fox News Digital , the Aug. 10 legal complaint stemmed from an August 2024 incident in which former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow was changing in the women's locker room and stripped down to her underwear when a recruit described as a "biological male who identifies as a woman" entered the room wearing a suit and tie. Grabow said that the recruit looked at her "as a man would look at a woman" before moving to another part of the locker room.

Grabow claimed that when she spoke to her superiors about her discomfort, she was told to "learn to deal with it" and "find another locker room" if she was uncomfortable.

San Francisco Ymca Changes Locker Room Rules After Transgender Controversy: Report

In addition to this incident, Grabow said that she and other concerned officers were told by police chief Mark Talbot that the "woman" hired by the department "will use the restroom that's appropriate for her gender" and were repeatedly instructed to refer to the recruit as "she."

Other officers also voiced concerns that they were not warned about sharing facilities with a biological male , something Talbot acknowledged could have been handled "better."

Appeals Court Revives Lawsuit By Alaska Airlines Flight Attendants Fired After Opposing Pride Message

Grabow later received an indefinite suspension pending termination in 2025 over a minor traffic violation committed prior to the incident after attempting to voice a complaint. Other officers have since left the department over their backlash to the transgender policy, the complaint states.

Grabow is seeking $15 million in compensatory damages, claiming Talbot and the police department were guilty of intentional infliction of emotional distress as well as violating her religious freedoms by forcing her to share a changing facility with a biological male and validate transgender ideology against her Catholic beliefs .

Christian Lifeguard Who Refused Pride Flag Duties And Was Suspended Is Now Headed Toward Trial

Attorney Scott Lloyd, who is representing Grabow in the case, told Fox News Digital in a statement that they are determined to protect female-only spaces through this case.

"We need to defend private spaces for the women who rely on them. Officer Grabow has done a brave and admirable thing by stepping forward, but it shouldn't have come to this," Lloyd said.

The Norfolk Police Department declined to comment to Fox News Digital, saying that it "cannot comment on pending litigation or personnel-related matters."

Under 2020 guidelines for the Norfolk Police Department, employees are encouraged not to question a transgender person's identity except for "articulable reasons," such as if they are related to a crime.

"Employees will respect an individual's gender identity and gender expression. An individual's gender expression may be traits that are not typically associated with a person's assigned sex at birth; these expressions may include wigs, prosthetics, makeup, adopted name, tone of voice, clothing, mannerisms, etc.," the 2020 general order read.

articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from £3m fund

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.

That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.

Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.

For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.

paragraphs: As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.
My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.
But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.
Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.
The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.
While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.
Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.
RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.
Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.
While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.
It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.
A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.
The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.
Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.
It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.
In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.
Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.
Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.
She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."
"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.
It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.
RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.
It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.
While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.
The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."
Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.
The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.
It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.
Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.
But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.
Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.
He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.
He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks
In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.
That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.
Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

articles.title: I was in so much pain I could barely feed my cats - now I'm back as a pro wrestler
articles.summary: The AEW star Jamie Hayter is set for two big shows in Glasgow and at Wembley Stadium in London this week.
articles.body:
Professional wrestling storylines are often built around surprise moments, from unexpected returns to sudden plot twists.

However when British star Jamie Hayter suffered two herniated discs in her back in 2023, she feared she would never get back in the ring.

It left her in constant pain, barely able to feed her cats - and wondering if her career was over.

But the grappler, who competes with All Elite Wrestling, told BBC News that the experience gave her a better perspective on her wrestling.

And the 31-year-old from Southampton is back on home turf this week, performing in two shows at Glasgow's OVO Hydro arena and then at AEW's biggest event of the year, called All In and held at Wembley Stadium on Sunday.

Her injury left her out of action for a year.

"The worst was the first few months because I was really unsure of things," she said.

"The pain was at its highest and I was bed bound – the most I could do was get up, feed my cats, make a coffee and then wobble back to bed.

"I was sitting there depressed, think I'm not doing anything, nothing is going on in my life, and it was hard to see a positive light. Weeks felt like they were taking years to go by.

"It helped me come back with a better mentality for wrestling than I had before, just more mellowed out and with a better understanding of what is worth getting upset over."

Hayter and her tag team partner, fellow Brit Alex Windsor, are in one of Sunday's featured bouts, challenging for the promotion's women's tag team titles in front of more than 40,000 people.

It comes about a decade after Hayter learned she had ADHD. She says her career of bumps and bruises is helping her cope with the diagnosis.

"It was not a surprise because my family are all neurodivergent and my siblings have autism," she recalls.

"At school someone would say 'oh, you might have ADHD' but it never went beyond that, other than getting a little extra help for exams which I always really struggled with.

"It was a relief being diagnosed at the end of the day. It meant I can understand my brain a little better, and how I process and work with things."

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The wrestler, real name Paige Woodling, says she can still find things overwhelming a lot of the time.

Being in the ring, though, has proved to be a help over the years, letting her "focus on one thing".

"I need to be in the zone with it, and I wish my brain could do that with other things too. But I think it mixes a lot of things together – there's an audience I want to entertain, it's my job, there are consequences if you don't do it well and I never want to let down the people who are there."

Given Hayter is regarded as one of the top wrestlers in AEW - the world's second biggest promotion behind industry giant World Wrestling Entertainment - it might seem unlikely that she would let down people.

Away from the squared circle though, and she admits things can be harder when the spotlights are off.

"You hear people say 'oh, being neurodivergent is my super power' and I hate that, because it's a debilitating thing. It can be a lot to deal with, and at points I do slip – I'll get overwhelmed with having places to be, or things to do, and life things go out the window.

"I'm still learning to manage it all better."

Hayter first fell in love with the industry when young, watching online clips and videos of matches, with brash anti-hero Stone Cold Steve Austin - a beer drinking, brawling and swearing star of the late 90s and early 2000s - an early inspiration.

"Nothing has ever captured me like wrestling did, not movies or TV or music," she says.

"Wrestling had this weird trance on me. I wanted to watch more, understand it and eventually do it, and I decided I was going to be a wrestler or a stuntwoman."

A prolific career on the British wrestling scene followed, which led to a stint in Japan, and a blink-and-you'll -miss-it appearance on WWE's development show NXT, where she lost to Scottish wrestler Piper Niven in Glasgow.

That was one of very few Scottish appearances for Hayter, who says she's eager to sample a "proper Glasgow crowd" at the Hydro, as AEW record their flagship TV shows Dynamite and Collision in the city.

She has been with the company since 2021, becoming a fixture of their women's division and winning the women's singles title on one occasion .

Earlier this year she was paired up with Norwich native Alex Windsor to form a team calling the Brawling Birds - a fan favourite duo fond of both brawls and booze.

"It's pretty close to us in real life, " she laughs.

"We're pretty tomboyish, we don't take things too seriously and we both like going to the pub. We're loud and boisterous but in a good way, and then you crank that up to 10 – we do ham it up a bit for an American audience."

After recovering from her debilitating injury, Hayter is now in far more optimistic spirits, chatting in the bar of a Glasgow hotel.

She jokes her onscreen character has varied inspirations from Farrah Fawcett in Charlie's Angels to Daphne in Scooby Doo, and this week's shows promise to be some of the biggest in her life.

Hayter also feels AEW itself could feature more women's wrestling - the promotion has yet to headline a major supercard with a women's match in its existence.

"Women in wrestling have proven themselves - we can do great matches, good promos and make you want to see a match.

"There's some inherent misogyny in wrestling as a whole, and women wrestlers for years would always get common tropes.

"But there are lots of different flavours of women's wrestling, and we can tap into that more."

Hayter herself says she's ready for any of those flavours, whatever comes next.

"I think I'm someone that just rolls with the punches. Whatever comes next I'll go full force with it."

Olympian Jones using ADHD diagnosis to box clever

'I wanted to be a dancer - now I'm a WWE star'

TV doctor says ADHD and OCD diagnoses have 'changed my life'

articles.title: The Voice Lindsay Clancy Says Told Her to Kill Lasted Just 18 Minutes. A Psychologist Says That’s ‘Very, Very Unusual’
articles.summary: Clancy is charged with the murders of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan
articles.body:
Lindsay Clancy is accused of intentionally killing her three young children

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis

A forensic psychologist testified that Clancy said a male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself"

A psychologist testified that Lindsay Clancy reported hearing a male voice for the first and only time during the roughly 18 minutes the killings of her three children occurred.

"She only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Kirk Heilbrun, who evaluated the mother of three, testified on Monday, August 24, the Boston Globe reported. "And to put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about."

Heilbrun told the court that Clancy said the male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

Heilbrun said the timing was unusual and said it could be a way to lessen her culpability.

Prosecutors allege Clancy deliberately strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023.

After killing the children, she jumped out of a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt, leaving her paralyzed.

Clancy, 36, does not deny she killed her children.

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the murders.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Heilbrun also testified that Clancy killed her children because she thought the children would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

During testimony on Tuesday, August 25, forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, testified that Clancy, who he interviewed twice in 2026, told him she first killed her son Dawson, then Cora and then her youngest child.

"All during this time where this voice is over and over, over again saying, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the children before you kill yourself," he testified.

Asked by a prosecutor if there was significance to the fact that the voice told her to kill the children, but did not tell her how to kill them, he responded, "Yes."

"You know, just like adults, children have a will to survive — a strong, strong will to survive. I think it's just part of being human," Saathoff said. "I mean, they are active. They can walk. They can run."

The closely watched four-week trial held in Plymouth County Superior Court has drawn national attention and sparked debate about postpartum mental health and the treatment of women experiencing psychiatric crises.

More than 70 witnesses have testified during the proceedings including medical experts, friends, law enforcement and Clancy's ex-husband Patrick.

articles.title: IndyCar’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix Promoter: ‘This Is My Sistine Chapel’
articles.summary: IndyCar's Freedom 250 Grand Prix Of Washington DC was an epic spectacle in the Nation's Capital. Forbes Sports Money provides a behind-the-scenes look at the...
articles.body:
There is a slogan in auto racing that best exemplifies the unbelievable 60-year success of Team Penske and Roger Penske's incredible accomplishments in business.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington DC was a perfect example of that slogan because Penske and IndyCar were able to create a sporting event in the National Mall of Washington, DC that was so stunning, so magical, and so well-orchestrated that it is hard to put it into words to someone who wasn't on the grounds.

It was the first auto racing ever held on the historic streets that surround the National Mall. Penske Corporation President Bud Denker was the man responsible for taking an impossible task and turning it into a moment of pride for IndyCar, the 150,000 spectators and 3,282,000 viewers that watched on FOX.

"I've never been on a journey like this in my life," Denker told me after the race. "I've been in a lot of deals, been in a lot of decisions. Been in a lot of sponsorship deals that were incredibly big, but I just can't ever imagine doing anything bigger than this.

"The Sistine Chapel was probably the most amazing thing that happened for Leonardo da Vinci.

Freedom 250 Grand Prix Gets Biggest Viewership For A Non-Indy 500 in Decades

It was the most-viewed non-Indy 500 race since the start of the IndyCar Series when the Indy Racing League and Champ Car merged before the 2008 season. It was up 364 percent over last year's 708,000 viewers for the FOX portion of last year's 15 th race from Portland, when the first 31 minutes started on FS1.

Sunday's viewership was up 279 percent with last year's 867,000 viewers for Sunday non-Indy 500 races on FOX.

The race partially overlapped with the NASCAR Cup race from New Hampshire which ran on USA from 2:14-6:36 pm.

The full race telecast averaged 1,686,000 viewers and the race peaked with 3,482,000 viewers from 2:30-2:45pm.

IndyCar on FOX is averaging 1,875,000 viewers through 15 races, up 32 percent vs. last year's season to date of 1,416,000 and up 70 percent over the 2024 season to date when 1,106,000 for races on NBC/USA/CNBC.

It was IndyCar's gift to the 250 th Birthday of the United States, but the positive reaction from those that came from around the world to witness the race may be IndyCar's biggest gift. Many of those fans had never attended an auto race before. Some left the race saying they were now IndyCar fans.

Freedom 250 On Track Action Driving Reaction

From a racing standpoint, Kyle Kirkwood dominated, winning the race after leading 128 laps of the 147-lap contest. There was plenty of action, though, throughout the field with 155 passes during the contest.

"It was racy. You could pass," said third-place finisher Will Power of Andretti Global. "A lot of my positions were gained just on-track passes. It was everything you'd want. Having an American President here watching the whole race, still there when I pulled up on the grid, you could see President Trump still watching, which meant that the race must have been pretty engaging, which is really good stuff. Great for the series."

I asked Power had what point in the day the moment of the magnitude of this spectacle hit him?

"Probably when we jumped in the truck and drove around," Power said. "You see the pageantry. It had a very Indy 500 vibe.

"I think IndyCar is in the best shape it's ever been in since I've been in the series. That's 21 years. It's just progressively gone up. More recently it's taken a big step. Really proud to be a part of it."

While some fans may look at the same driver leading 128 laps in front of the field with a negative reaction, the value of this event wasn't necessarily what happened on the track, it was having IndyCar as the star attraction for a huge crowd in a setting unlike any other.

It wasn't the Indianapolis 500, where 350,000 fans jam the Indianapolis Motor Speedway for the world's most famous and historic race. But for a street race near the end of the summer celebrating a milestone moment in the history of the United States that drew 150,000 enthusiastic fans, it was a major event for both IndyCar and the USA.

"This morning when I woke up, quite honestly, there's an instinct that you have when you wake up and your heart is already racing," the race-winner said. "I only get that one other place, and that's the Indy 500. Just that sensation, it gives it its own energy. That's what this place had.

"This was a very special day. We were very prepared for it. Outside of the Indy 500, I don't think there's another race that you'd want to win."

Freedom 250 Grand Prix One Last Celebration Of The 250th Birthday Of The United States

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, DC was historic for where it was being held. The US Capitol Building in the background behind the flag stand and other iconic structures such as the National Archives, the Washington Monument, the National Archives and other famed attractions made it a spectacular setting.

Every branch of the United States Military was honored with each branch's marching band performing on the track. There were seven military flyovers during the event including the B2 Stealth Bomber and a special flyover from Air Force One escorted by F-15 Eagles and F-15 Fighting Falcons.

Freedom 250 Grand Prix Was IndyCar's American Dream

Denker and his team were able to create a spectacle out of something many critics didn't believe would ever happen. He started a lengthy lobbying effort that began in August 2025 with 81 meetings on Capitol Hill trying to get it approved by the United States House of Representatives and US Senate.

On January 21, the project was at an impasse. There wasn't enough support to get approval for the areas of the National Mall that were required to put up a temporary street circuit.

Denker told Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy that he was pulling the plug, that the race wouldn't happen. Duffy encouraged Denker to hold off because he had another plan.

He was able to get an Executive Order from President Donald J. Trump on January 30.

That's when the hard work began to plan the event, and secure the proper permits and licenses required because of all the different jurisdictions involved.

"If you asked anybody in this town, or I would say on our industry, could we have a race in Washington, D.C. a year ago, the answer would have been, 'are you crazy?'" Denker told me. "That is what most of them said when I first came up here a year ago.

"But I didn't think it was a crazy idea.

"Resiliency, I think, is the key word for me. Persistence is the other piece. And don't take no, because there are a lot of 'no's' here.

"People have this phrase, 'Penske Perfect.' We're never perfect, but we're not going to have people think we are. That's pretty good to me, and many people thought this was perfect. And for a first -time event, my team made a flawless execution."

Although he is the Penske Corporation President and works out of the corporate offices near Detroit, Denker spent most of his time living in Washington, DC beginning last August. He was running solo until March, trying to put the event together.

Denker said it the race was really put together with his full team beginning in June, which meant it had to be ready to go in a little over two full months.

Could The Freedom 250 Grand Prix Return to Washington DC In The Future?

President Trump, Washington, DC Mayor Muriel Bowser and many other government officials want the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to be back on the IndyCar schedule in future years. But this race was originally created as a one-time-only event to help celebrate the 250 th birthday of the United States.

The Penske Corporation invested $35 million to make this event happen. Although 150,000 fans came on Sunday with 214,000 fans for the two-day weekend, tickets were free and distributed through a lottery system from the 288,000 requests that were submitted.

Revenue came from the sale of lavish VIP suites and from an impressive list of corporation sponsors. Merchandise sales were impressive with lines of spectators buying up all the Freedom 250 Grand Prix merchandise they could find. According to Denker, $900,000 of merchandise was sold on Saturday alone. At the Grand Prix of Arlington, $900,000 of merchandise was sold over the weekend for a first-time event.

For it to become an annual event, the business structure would have to generate significant revenue.

"We have a difficult choice to make," Denker said. "The question is this. How many people would come back again for the event in Year Two, a non-anniversary year for the United States? Could you charge tickets, a price for tickets, to cover some of the revenue and the loss you have because this is so expensive? Is it $50 a person? What would that do to the crowd?

"Or did you tease them enough this year enough this year that they really would want to come back and would come back also by paying something that's reasonable?

"That's the questions we have to look at. And I think the key thing for us is to probably talk to our sponsors and say, is there interest in coming back?

"But ultimately, it's a Roger Penske decision. We'll make that decision pretty soon."

Denker sat with Penske and his wife, Kathy, in the Presidential Suite throughout the race and expressed his appreciation and gratitude for what the event meant to him and his family.

"This is my crowning achievement," Denker said. "Roger has had a lot of crowning achievements in his life, many more than I have, but it won't get better for me. I know this is one of the top ones for Roger."

This event was about Patriotism, and the fans that came to the race were happy to be part of the celebration and turned the National Mall into one of the "happiest places on Earth" at least for one day.

Penske showed his appreciation to the fans by taking out a full-page ad in The Washington Post on Tuesday with the following letter:

"To Our Fans, Thank you for making the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C., such an extraordinary and memorable event for our nation.

"The energy and enthusiasm you brought to our nation's capital made this weekend truly special. Whether you joined us in Washington or watched from home, your passion for INDYCAR and motorsports was on full display and helped create a celebration worthy of America's 250th anniversary.

"We are grateful to President Trump and his Administration for their leadership and support in making this historic event possible. We also thank Mayor Bowser and the broader team in Washington, D.C., for their partnership and for working together with our organization to bring the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to life in our Nation's Capital.

"The Freedom 250 Grand Prix brought together the speed, competition and pageantry of INDYCAR racing with an incredible celebration of our country. "I also want to thank all of our INDYCAR drivers and teams for delivering an outstanding weekend of competition and congratulate Kyle Kirkwood on his victory in the Freedom 250 Grand Prix.

"We are also grateful to the many brands and partners whose support helped make this historic event possible, including Monumental Sports & Entertainment and Harbinger. Their commitment and collaboration were instrumental in bringing this ambitious vision to life.

"As we celebrate America's 250th anniversary, all of us at INDYCAR are incredibly proud to have played a part in this historic occasion.

"Most importantly, thank you again to our fans. Your passion is what drives our sport forward, and we could not be prouder to have shared this unforgettable celebration of America and INDYCAR with you.

"Roger Penske, Chairman of Penske Entertainment"

It's likely the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington DC may be the only time a street race is held in the Nation's Capital on the streets around the National Mall. It certainly provided a "Once in a Lifetime" event for those who attended, giving Denker and his team his "Sistine Chapel" moment.

"The Sistine Chapel was probably the most amazing thing that happened for Leonardo da Vinci.

It was the most-viewed non-Indy 500 race since the start of the IndyCar Series when the Indy Racing League and Champ Car merged before the 2008 season. It was up 364 percent over last year's 708,000 viewers for the FOX portion of last year's 15 th race from Portland, when the first 31 minutes started on FS1.
Sunday's viewership was up 279 percent with last year's 867,000 viewers for Sunday non-Indy 500 races on FOX.
The race partially overlapped with the NASCAR Cup race from New Hampshire which ran on USA from 2:14-6:36 pm.
The full race telecast averaged 1,686,000 viewers and the race peaked with 3,482,000 viewers from 2:30-2:45pm.

IndyCar on FOX is averaging 1,875,000 viewers through 15 races, up 32 percent vs. last year's season to date of 1,416,000 and up 70 percent over the 2024 season to date when 1,106,000 for races on NBC/USA/CNBC.

articles.title: Morte de irmãos: quem eram o jogador e estudante vítimas de acidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Adolescentes de 13 e 17 anos estavam em carro que capotou com a família na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP). Mãe e prima continuam internadas.
articles.summary: Adolescentes de 13 e 17 anos estavam em carro que capotou com a família na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro. Mãe e prima continuam internadas.
articles.body:
As mortes trágicas do jogador de futebol Felipe Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 anos, e de sua irmã, a estudante Beatriz Siqueira, de 17 , geraram forte comoção no interior de São Paulo e no ABC Paulista. Felipe era considerado um atleta promissor e Beatriz uma estudante muito querida por colegas e professores. (Veja mais abaixo).

Os adolescentes estavam em um carro que capotou com a família na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP), no domingo (23). A mãe e a prima deles continuam internadas.

📱 Siga o g1 São Carlos e Araraquara no Instagram

Com a presença de dezenas de pessoas, os corpos dos irmãos foram velados na terça-feira (25) no Ginásio Poliesportivo de São Bernardo do Campo e sepultados no Cemitério Cristo Redentor, em Santo André (SP).

Amigos, familiares, equipes de futebol e a comunidade escolar prestaram diversas homenagens nas redes sociais. (Veja mais abaixo).

O QUE SE SABE: veja como foi acidente que matou jogador de futebol e a irmã em SP

DESPEDIDA: Mortes de jogador de futebol e irmã em acidente causam comoção em SP

Felipe Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 anos, atuava no sub-14 do Mauá Futebol Clube; ele morreu em acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro — Foto: @maia_fotoo/Instagram

Felipe era jogador de futebol de base e atuava como atleta do Mauá Futebol Clube na categoria sub-14. Em nota de pesar emitida pela diretoria do clube nas redes sociais, a equipe lamentou a perda do jovem.

"Felipe fazia parte da Família Mauá Futebol e, mesmo tão jovem, já deixava sua marca dentro e fora de campo, com sua alegria e talento , compartilhando conosco momentos que permanecerão para sempre em nossa memória".

"Irmão, está difícil encontrar forças para superar. Eu ainda não consigo acreditar que isso aconteceu. Pra mim é um sonho que logo vai passar. Eu ainda to esperando uma mensagem sua falando que tá bem. (...) Você é insubstituível, ninguém nesse momento consegue entender o porquê disso, eu te amo muito meu IRMÃO, vai fazer muita falta", escreveu Andrei Domingues, colega de time de Felipe.

Na temporada passada, Felipe defendeu as cores do Esporte Clube União Suzano (ECUS SAF), onde foi capitão da categoria Sub-13. O clube também emitiu nota manifestando solidariedade aos familiares.

Estudantes queridos pela comunidade escolar

Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 17 anos, morreu em acidente com o irmão Felipe na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Além dos gramados, os irmãos compartilhavam a rotina de estudos no Darwin International School, em São Bernardo do Campo. O colégio publicou uma mensagem de despedida ressaltando o impacto positivo deixado por ambos entre colegas e professores.

"Ficam as lembranças, os sorrisos, as histórias, os momentos compartilhados e a presença de Beatriz e Felipe na vida de tantos colegas, professores e educadores que tiveram o privilégio de caminhar ao lado deles".

Nas redes sociais, mensagens de familiares e amigos próximos destacaram o afeto pelos adolescentes. " Que falta vocês farão na nossa vida , que buraco vocês deixaram no nosso peito (...) Iremos amar vocês pro resto da vida", escreveu uma familiar em publicação.

"É impossível encontrar palavras para expressar a dor de perder dois alunos tão queridos. Fica o vazio, a saudade e a lembrança de cada sorriso e de cada momento vivido. Que Deus conforte o coração da família! 🙏🏽😔", escreveu a professora Adriana Tinonin.

Amigos da família também manifestaram apoio aos pais e familiares pedindo orações.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 13h26 de domingo (23) na pista sul da Rodovia Anhanguera (SP-330), na altura do km 241, em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro.

O veículo Fiat Fastback ocupado pela família retornava de uma viagem a Barretos (SP) quando capotou.

Segundo a Artesp, o motorista perdeu o controle da direção, entrou no canteiro central, chocou-se contra a defensa metálica e capotou sobre o elemento de drenagem.

As causas exatas ainda estão sendo apuradas pela Polícia Civil. Uma testemunha que dirigia outro veículo e presenciou o fato relatou aos policiais rodoviários que não havia nenhum outro automóvel ou objeto na pista que pudesse ter causado a colisão.

O motorista também confirmou ter perdido o controle do veículo sem nenhuma interferência externa. A Polícia Científica esteve no local para realizar a perícia técnica.

Carro de família ficou destruído após capotagem em grave acidente na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: CCM Artesp

O motorista foi submetido ao teste do etilômetro (bafômetro) no local, com resultado de 0,00 mg/l de álcool no sangue, descartando o uso de bebida alcoólica.

O acidente foi registrado como homicídio culposo (sem intenção) na direção de veículo automotor e lesão corporal culposa (sem intenção) na direção de veículo automotor, e é investigado pela Polícia Civil de Santa Rita do Passa Quatro.

Outras três pessoas que estavam no veículo sofreram ferimentos e foram socorridas:

Maria Fernanda Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 46 ano s (esposa do motorista e mãe dos irmãos): teve ferimentos graves, deu entrada no hospital consciente e passou por cirurgia em uma unidade de saúde de Ribeirão Preto (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.

Lorena Conte Barbosa Barros de Marco, de 14 anos (sobrinha do motorista): deu entrada em estado grave, inconsciente, precisou ser intubada e está internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) de um hospital de Campinas (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.

Luiz Fernando Barbosa de Barros, de 51 anos (motorista e pai dos irmãos): sofreu lesões leves.

Jogador de futebol Felipe Siqueira, de 13 anos, e a irmã, Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 17, morreram em grave acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Amigos, familiares, equipes de futebol e a comunidade escolar prestaram diversas homenagens nas redes sociais. (Veja mais abaixo).
O QUE SE SABE: veja como foi acidente que matou jogador de futebol e a irmã em SP
DESPEDIDA: Mortes de jogador de futebol e irmã em acidente causam comoção em SP
Felipe Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 13 anos, atuava no sub-14 do Mauá Futebol Clube; ele morreu em acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro — Foto: @maia_fotoo/Instagram

Felipe era jogador de futebol de base e atuava como atleta do Mauá Futebol Clube na categoria sub-14. Em nota de pesar emitida pela diretoria do clube nas redes sociais, a equipe lamentou a perda do jovem.

"Felipe fazia parte da Família Mauá Futebol e, mesmo tão jovem, já deixava sua marca dentro e fora de campo, com sua alegria e talento , compartilhando conosco momentos que permanecerão para sempre em nossa memória".

"Irmão, está difícil encontrar forças para superar. Eu ainda não consigo acreditar que isso aconteceu. Pra mim é um sonho que logo vai passar. Eu ainda to esperando uma mensagem sua falando que tá bem. (...) Você é insubstituível, ninguém nesse momento consegue entender o porquê disso, eu te amo muito meu IRMÃO, vai fazer muita falta", escreveu Andrei Domingues, colega de time de Felipe.
Na temporada passada, Felipe defendeu as cores do Esporte Clube União Suzano (ECUS SAF), onde foi capitão da categoria Sub-13. O clube também emitiu nota manifestando solidariedade aos familiares.
Estudantes queridos pela comunidade escolar
Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 17 anos, morreu em acidente com o irmão Felipe na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Além dos gramados, os irmãos compartilhavam a rotina de estudos no Darwin International School, em São Bernardo do Campo. O colégio publicou uma mensagem de despedida ressaltando o impacto positivo deixado por ambos entre colegas e professores.

"Ficam as lembranças, os sorrisos, as histórias, os momentos compartilhados e a presença de Beatriz e Felipe na vida de tantos colegas, professores e educadores que tiveram o privilégio de caminhar ao lado deles".

Nas redes sociais, mensagens de familiares e amigos próximos destacaram o afeto pelos adolescentes. " Que falta vocês farão na nossa vida , que buraco vocês deixaram no nosso peito (...) Iremos amar vocês pro resto da vida", escreveu uma familiar em publicação.

"É impossível encontrar palavras para expressar a dor de perder dois alunos tão queridos. Fica o vazio, a saudade e a lembrança de cada sorriso e de cada momento vivido. Que Deus conforte o coração da família! 🙏🏽😔", escreveu a professora Adriana Tinonin.
Amigos da família também manifestaram apoio aos pais e familiares pedindo orações.
O acidente aconteceu por volta das 13h26 de domingo (23) na pista sul da Rodovia Anhanguera (SP-330), na altura do km 241, em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro.
O veículo Fiat Fastback ocupado pela família retornava de uma viagem a Barretos (SP) quando capotou.
Segundo a Artesp, o motorista perdeu o controle da direção, entrou no canteiro central, chocou-se contra a defensa metálica e capotou sobre o elemento de drenagem.

As causas exatas ainda estão sendo apuradas pela Polícia Civil. Uma testemunha que dirigia outro veículo e presenciou o fato relatou aos policiais rodoviários que não havia nenhum outro automóvel ou objeto na pista que pudesse ter causado a colisão.
O motorista também confirmou ter perdido o controle do veículo sem nenhuma interferência externa. A Polícia Científica esteve no local para realizar a perícia técnica.
Carro de família ficou destruído após capotagem em grave acidente na Rodovia Anhanguera em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: CCM Artesp
O motorista foi submetido ao teste do etilômetro (bafômetro) no local, com resultado de 0,00 mg/l de álcool no sangue, descartando o uso de bebida alcoólica.

O acidente foi registrado como homicídio culposo (sem intenção) na direção de veículo automotor e lesão corporal culposa (sem intenção) na direção de veículo automotor, e é investigado pela Polícia Civil de Santa Rita do Passa Quatro.
Outras três pessoas que estavam no veículo sofreram ferimentos e foram socorridas:

Maria Fernanda Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 46 ano s (esposa do motorista e mãe dos irmãos): teve ferimentos graves, deu entrada no hospital consciente e passou por cirurgia em uma unidade de saúde de Ribeirão Preto (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.

Lorena Conte Barbosa Barros de Marco, de 14 anos (sobrinha do motorista): deu entrada em estado grave, inconsciente, precisou ser intubada e está internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) de um hospital de Campinas (SP). Não há informações sobre o estado de saúde atual dela.
Luiz Fernando Barbosa de Barros, de 51 anos (motorista e pai dos irmãos): sofreu lesões leves.
Jogador de futebol Felipe Siqueira, de 13 anos, e a irmã, Beatriz Siqueira Barbosa de Barros, de 17, morreram em grave acidente em Santa Rita do Passa Quatro (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

articles.title: Ilha particular com forte é colocada à venda na Itália por R$ 33 mi | G1
articles.standfirst: Propriedade de 5,7 mil m² fica na Lagoa de Veneza, no norte do país, e tem uma fortificação erguida em 1806. Ilha também conta com casa, jardins e pontos para atracar barcos.
articles.summary: Propriedade de 5,7 mil m² fica na Lagoa de Veneza, no norte da Itália, e tem uma fortificação erguida em 1806. Ilha também conta com casa, jardins e pontos para atracar barcos.
articles.body:
Ilha Crevan, na Itália, está à venda por R$ 33 milhões — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard

Uma ilha particular com uma fortificação construída há mais de 200 anos foi colocada à venda na Lagoa de Veneza, no norte da Itália , por € 5,5 milhões (cerca de R$ 33 milhões ). Veja fotos mais abaixo.

✅ Siga o canal de notícias internacionais do g1 no WhatsApp

A Ilha de Crevan tem 5,7 mil metros quadrados e fica a cerca de 7 km do centro de Veneza. A propriedade está em uma área mais isolada da lagoa, com vista para Burano e Torcello, duas das ilhas que compõem o arquipélago veneziano.

O principal imóvel da ilha é um antigo forte militar de 215 m² construído em 1806, durante o domínio de Napoleão Bonaparte sobre a região. A estrutura deixou de ter função militar depois da Primeira Guerra Mundial.

Desde então, a ilha passou para proprietários particulares. A fortificação foi restaurada no fim da década de 1990 e adaptada para uso residencial.

A propriedade tem quatro quartos e dois banheiros, além de aquecimento e ar-condicionado. Também há um canal interno, dois pontos privativos para atracar barcos e um heliponto.

A maior parte da propriedade é ocupada por áreas verdes, com árvores, jardins, gramados e árvores frutíferas. O acesso à casa é feito por caminhos dentro da ilha.

A localização permite chegar a Veneza de barco. Crevan fica em uma região mais afastada do fluxo turístico do centro histórico da cidade.

A venda é anunciada pela imobiliária italiana Lionard Luxury Real Estate. Segundo a empresa, o imóvel reúne características pouco comuns no mercado: uma ilha particular, uma construção militar histórica e proximidade com Veneza.

Forte napoleônico em ilha que está à venda na Itália — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard

A fortificação de Crevan surgiu durante o período em que Veneza estava sob domínio francês. Napoleão havia ocupado a cidade em 1797, encerrando a antiga República de Veneza.

A construção do forte, em 1806, fez parte de um conjunto de estruturas militares criadas para proteger a lagoa. Depois, durante o domínio austríaco, a fortificação foi ampliada e reforçada.

Em 1866, a região passou a fazer parte do Reino da Itália, e Crevan continuou a ter função militar por décadas. Depois da Primeira Guerra Mundial, o uso militar foi encerrado, e a propriedade acabou passando para proprietários particulares.

A Lionard Luxury Real Estate informou que a restauração iniciada em 1996 procurou preservar a configuração original da construção, mas adaptou o interior do forte para a utilização como residência.

Ilha Crevan à venda na Itália — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard

Ilha à venda na Itália tem pontos para atracar barcos e estrutura para receber helicópteros — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard

Vista da Ilha de Crevan, que está à venda na Itála — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard

Ilha tem vista para áreas turísticas de Veneza — Foto: Courtesy of Lionard
